docs.text: Driver PCAL9555 Driver ¶ A C++20 driver for the NXP PCA9555 and PCAL9555A 16-bit I2C GPIO expanders. It drives outputs, reads inputs and interrupt sources, and on the PCAL9555A sets drive strength, pull resistors, input latches and open-drain ports, on any MCU. Quickstart API guide Source on GitHub The driver has no platform code. You give it a small class that brings the bus up and moves bytes; it does the rest: the presence and identity checks, the register pairs, the write order that avoids glitches, and a copy of every register so that a pin change is one transfer, and the check that finds a power-on reset before a stale copy is written over it. 16-bit I2C GPIO expander PCA9555 / PCAL9555A NXP Semiconductors Function 16 I/O pins in two 8-pin ports; each pin an input or a latched output, with input polarity inversion Interface I2C up to 400 kHz; 7-bit address 0x20 to 0x27 from the A2, A1 and A0 pins Interrupt Open-drain INT on any input change, cleared by reading the input port Agile I/O (PCAL9555A) Four drive strengths per pin, 100 kΩ pull-up or pull-down per pin, input latch, interrupt mask and status, push-pull or open-drain per port Supply PCA9555 2.3 V to 5.5 V; PCAL9555A 1.65 V to 5.5 V What you get ¶ One object per chip. PCAL9555<YourPort> takes your port, the address and a Config , and does no I/O until EnsureInitialized() . See API guide . Both parts, one API. Config::variant names the part; on a PCA9555 the Agile I/O calls return Unsupported without touching the bus. See Agile I/O . Errors you can act on. Every call returns Result<T> with an Error such as Bus , DeviceIdMismatch or Unsupported . See API guide . Datasheet defaults. Config{} holds the power-up value of every register. See Configuration . A tiny port. Three bus hooks and an optional log hook, checked by a concept at compile time. The chip needs no delays and has no reset pin. See Porting . No heap, no exceptions, no RTTI. The host tests build with -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti . See Contract . Tested without hardware. Host tests run the driver against a protocol model of the chip, with every bus transfer failed in turn. See Testing and CI . docs.text: Agile I/O ¶ The PCAL9555A's additions to the PCA9555: output drive strength, pull resistors, input latch, interrupt mask and status, and open-drain ports. Section numbers refer to the PCAL9555A data sheet (Rev. 2). Datasheet sections this page relies on Registers and command bytes: NXP PCAL9555A Rev. 2, 6.2 Registers; 6.2.1 Pointer register and command byte, p. 5 Output drive strength: NXP PCAL9555A Rev. 2, 6.2.6 Output drive strength register pairs; 8.2 Output drive strength control, p. 9 Input latch: NXP PCAL9555A Rev. 2, 6.2.7 Input latch register pair, p. 9 Pull-up and pull-down resistors: NXP PCAL9555A Rev. 2, 6.2.8 Pull-up/pull-down enable register pair; 6.2.9 Pull-up/pull-down selection register pair, p. 10 Interrupt mask: NXP PCAL9555A Rev. 2, 6.2.10 Interrupt mask register pair, p. 11 Interrupt status: NXP PCAL9555A Rev. 2, 6.2.11 Interrupt status register pair, p. 12 Open-drain ports and the 0x4F write order: NXP PCAL9555A Rev. 2, 6.2.12 Output port configuration register (4Fh), p. 12 Pull resistor value, sink current and logic levels: NXP PCAL9555A Rev. 2, 12 Static characteristics, p. 26 Registers, command bytes and power-up values: NXP PCA9555 Rev. 10, 6.2 Registers; 6.2.1 Command byte (Table 4), p. 6 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map . Which part is fitted ¶ The two parts are pin compatible and the PCAL9555A answers every PCA9555 register the same way, so a board may carry either. The driver does not detect the part (neither data sheet says how a PCA9555 answers the Agile I/O command bytes): Config::variant names it. Config::variant Registers used Agile I/O calls Agile I/O Config fields Variant::Pca9555 (default) 0x00 to 0x07 Unsupported , nothing sent Must keep their power-up value, else Unsupported Variant::Pcal9555a 0x00 to 0x07 and 0x40 to 0x4F Work Written and read back by EnsureInitialized() Pca9555 is safe on both parts: a PCAL9555A driven that way keeps its Agile I/O registers at their power-up values (pull-ups on, interrupts masked, full drive, push-pull). Pcal9555a on a PCA9555 fails the start-up before any write ( Hardware ). pcal9555 :: Error SetUpButtons ( Expander & io ) { constexpr uint16_t kButtons = 0xF000 ; // P1_4..P1_7, to ground if ( auto r = io . SetPull ( kButtons , pcal9555 :: Pull :: Up ); ! r ) { return r . error ; // Unsupported on a driver configured for the PCA9555 } if ( auto r = io . SetInputLatch ( kButtons , true ); ! r ) { // a short press is not lost return r . error ; } return io . SetInterruptEnabled ( kButtons , true ). error ; // INT falls on a press } Drive strength ¶ Section 6.2.6. Each output has four drive levels, two bits per pin in 0x40 to 0x43. A lower level slows the edges and reduces ground bounce and EMI on lightly loaded lines; it also lowers the current the pin can sink. DriveStrength Code Of full drive Quarter 00b 0.25 Half 01b 0.5 ThreeQuarters 10b 0.75 Full 11b 1 (power-up) SetDriveStrength(mask, level) writes both drive strength pairs. In Config , drive_strength_codes holds the codes in the register layout, pin n at bits 2n+1..2n; DriveStrengthAll(level) builds a value with every pin at one level. pcal9555 :: Error QuietLeds ( Expander & io ) { // Less drive, slower edges, less ground bounce: LEDs on port 0 at a quarter of full drive. if ( auto r = io . SetDriveStrength ( 0x00FF , pcal9555 :: DriveStrength :: Quarter ); ! r ) { return r . error ; } return io . SetOutputMode ( pcal9555 :: Bank :: Port1 , pcal9555 :: OutputMode :: OpenDrain ). error ; } Pull resistors ¶ Sections 6.2.8 and 6.2.9. Each pin has a 100 kΩ (50 kΩ to 150 kΩ) resistor that can pull up, pull down or be disconnected; at power-up every pin has its pull-up on. Pull Enable bit (0x46, 0x47) Selection bit (0x48, 0x49) None 0 unchanged Up 1 1 Down 1 0 SetPull() writes the selection before the enable, so that a pin switched from "off" to "down" never pulls up in between. A port in open-drain mode disconnects its resistors whatever these registers say. Input latch ¶ Section 6.2.7. Without the latch an input that changes and changes back before it is read leaves no trace: INT releases and the input register shows the current level. With the latch on ( SetInputLatch(mask, true) ), the input register keeps the level that raised the interrupt, and INT stays asserted, until the input port is read; the next read shows the pin again. Use it for short pulses such as button presses or a sensor's data-ready strobe. Interrupt mask and status ¶ Sections 6.2.10 and 6.2.11. At power-up every pin is masked: unlike the PCA9555, a PCAL9555A raises no interrupt until SetInterruptEnabled(mask, true) clears mask bits. Unmasking a pin whose change is still pending asserts INT at once. ReadInterruptStatus() returns the pins that raised the interrupt; masked pins read 0. Reading the status does not clear the interrupt; reading the input port does. Output mode ¶ Section 6.2.12. SetOutputMode(Bank::Port0 or Bank::Port1, mode) selects push-pull or open-drain for a whole port (ODEN0, ODEN1 in 0x4F). An open-drain output only pulls low; a "high" output lets the line float to an external pull-up, for wired-OR lines or a load on another supply. The data sheet recommends setting 0x4F before the configuration registers make the pins outputs; EnsureInitialized() and ApplyConfig() write it in that order, and a SetOutputMode() call should come before the SetDirection() call. Not verified on hardware ¶ The behaviour above is the data sheet's, checked against the protocol model in the host tests. On a bench, with a PCAL9555A at 0x20: SetDriveStrength(PinMask(0), DriveStrength::Quarter) with P0_0 an output toggling into 50 pF: the edges are slower than at Full on an oscilloscope. With P1_0 an input and nothing connected, SetPull(PinMask(8), Pull::Down) makes ReadPin(8) read low, Pull::Up high. With P1_0 latched and unmasked, a 10 µs low pulse on it asserts INT, and the next ReadInputs() shows bit 8 low once, then high. With port 1 open-drain, a 10 kΩ pull-up to 3.3 V on P1_0 and the output "high", the pin reads 3.3 V; "low" pulls it to ground.

API guide ¶ The driver's API by task, with code that compiles: start, drive outputs, read inputs, handle an interrupt, stop and handle errors. The PCAL9555A extras have their own page, Agile I/O . Datasheet sections this page relies on Input, output, polarity inversion and configuration registers: NXP PCAL9555A Rev. 2, 6.2.2 to 6.2.5 Input port, Output port, Polarity inversion and Configuration register pairs, p. 7 Interrupt status: NXP PCAL9555A Rev. 2, 6.2.11 Interrupt status register pair, p. 12 Power-on reset: NXP PCAL9555A Rev. 2, 6.4 Power-on reset; 8.3 Power-on reset requirements, p. 13 Interrupt output (INT): NXP PCAL9555A Rev. 2, 6.5 Interrupt output, p. 14 Power-on reset: NXP PCA9555 Rev. 10, 6.3 Power-on reset, p. 8 Interrupt output (INT), no mask or status: NXP PCA9555 Rev. 10, 6.5.3 Interrupt output, p. 14 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map . The shape of the API ¶ Group Calls Lifecycle EnsureInitialized() , IsInitialized() , Deinitialize() Configuration ApplyConfig() , GetConfig() , GetAddress() Pins (both parts) SetDirection() , SetOutputs() , WriteOutputs() , ToggleOutputs() , SetPolarityInversion() , ReadInputs() , ReadPin() Agile I/O (PCAL9555A) SetDriveStrength() , SetPull() , SetInputLatch() , SetInterruptEnabled() , ReadInterruptStatus() , SetOutputMode() Free functions Validate() , PinMask() , AddressFromPins() , DriveStrengthAll() , ToString() , GetDriverVersion() Every call that touches the chip returns Result<T> : check ok() (or the bool conversion) and read value , or read error . Result is [[nodiscard]] , so an unchecked call is a compiler warning. A failed call's value is T{} , never a stale or partial reading. Pins are numbered 0 to 15: 0 to 7 are P0_0 to P0_7, 8 to 15 are P1_0 to P1_7. The calls that change pins take a mask, bit n for pin n ( PinMask(n) ), and change only the pins in it; a mask of 0 is InvalidArgument . Start ¶ constexpr pcal9555 :: Config Agile () { pcal9555 :: Config c {}; c . variant = pcal9555 :: Variant :: Pcal9555a ; return c ; } pcal9555 :: Error BringUp ( Expander & io ) { // Expander io(port, 0x20, Agile()); stores the configuration, no I/O. const auto r = io . EnsureInitialized (); // first call starts the chip; then Ok, no I/O if ( ! r ) { std :: printf ( "PCAL9555A start: %s 
 " , pcal9555 :: ToString ( r . error )); // the next call retries } return r . error ; } The constructor stores the port, the address and the configuration and does no I/O. EnsureInitialized() is the one way to start the chip. Its first call checks the configuration ( Validate() ) and the address, brings the bus up, reads the input ports to see that a part ACKs, on a PCAL9555A reads 0x4F and checks that its reserved bits are 0, then writes every register of the configuration and reads each back. A register that does not hold what was written means another part answers at the address: DeviceIdMismatch . Once it has succeeded, EnsureInitialized() returns Ok at once with no I/O, so a caller (or a handler that owns the driver) can call it before every use. After a failure the driver stays uninitialised and the next call starts again from the beginning. No other call starts the chip: before EnsureInitialized() succeeds every read and write returns NotInitialized and sends nothing. ApplyConfig() before the start only stores the configuration for the first EnsureInitialized() . The chip has no reset, so the start-up writes every register instead: the result is the same whatever the chip held before, a power-up or a previous run of the firmware. Drive outputs ¶ pcal9555 :: Error DriveRelays ( Expander & io ) { constexpr uint16_t kRelays = 0x000F ; // P0_0..P0_3 if ( auto r = io . SetOutputs ( kRelays , false ); ! r ) { // level first: off return r . error ; } if ( auto r = io . SetDirection ( kRelays , pcal9555 :: Direction :: Output ); ! r ) { return r . error ; } return io . ToggleOutputs ( pcal9555 :: PinMask ( 2 )). error ; // relay 2 on, one write } Call Register pair Effect SetOutputs(mask, high) Output port Pins in mask high or low WriteOutputs(high_mask) Output port All 16 at once ToggleOutputs(mask) Output port Pins in mask inverted SetDirection(mask, Direction::Output) 0x4F, output port, configuration Pins in mask drive their output value Set the level before the direction: a pin that becomes an output drives its output latch at once, and the latch is high after power-up. The output latch is kept for input pins, so it can be prepared while the pin is still an input. SetDirection() is the one pin call that sends more than its own register. A pin that becomes an output drives its latch through its port's output stage, and a power-on reset sets every latch high and every stage push-pull (table 4). So it first checks for a reset (one read, see Recover after a power loss ), then writes from the driver's copy in the data sheet's order (section 6.2.12): 0x4F on a PCAL9555A, the output pair, the configuration pair. Whatever the chip went through, no pin becomes an output at a level or stage you did not set. It costs one read and two write pairs on a PCA9555, plus a 1-byte write on a PCAL9555A (about 0.3 ms at 400 kHz instead of 90 µs); call it at configuration time, not in a fast loop. Releasing pins ( Direction::Input ) is the safe direction, and the cheapest. When every pin ends up an input, the configuration pair is the only transfer: no check, nothing before it that could fail, since nothing can be driven whatever the chip went through. When other pins stay outputs, the reset check comes first, then the configuration pair, so the pins are released by the first write, then 0x4F and the output pair for the remaining outputs. The driver keeps a copy of every register it wrote ( GetConfig() ), computes the new pair from it and writes the pair in one transfer, without reading it first: by default a pin call other than SetDirection() is the one 3-byte write the data sheet needs and nothing more. Read-back is chosen per call: every setter takes a last argument Verify , Verify::None by default. With Verify::ReadBack the call then reads the pair back, a 2-byte read that more than doubles its bus time, and a write the chip acknowledged but did not keep returns Error::WriteMismatch . An acknowledge carries no checksum, and the data sheet allows for a glitch or data corruption (section 8.3); the output port reads back the value it holds, not the pin (section 6.2.3), so the read-back shows what the chip will drive. Pass Verify::ReadBack on the calls where a lost write matters more than the bus time, such as a driver enable, and leave the hot path at the default. A write whose transfer failed ( Bus , NoDevice ) may still have reached the chip: the bytes can be stored before a lost ACK or a NACK of the last byte. So after a failed write the copy does not keep the old value as if nothing happened. It takes the riskier of the old and the asked value, and the register is marked unknown: Register pair The copy after a failed write Configuration ( input_mask ) A pin that was or was asked to be an output counts as an output (old AND asked) Output port ( output_high_mask ) The written level Drive strength ( drive_strength_codes ) The stronger code of each pin 0x4F ( port0_mode , port1_mode ) Push-pull if either was push-pull Polarity, input latch, pull enable and selection, interrupt mask The written value The next call that builds on an unknown register first reads it from the chip into the copy (one more read, only after a failure), so it never computes a new value from a stale one; a successful write of the pair, a read-back call ( ReadOutputLatch() , ReadInputMask() , ReadPolarityInversion() ), ApplyConfig() and EnsureInitialized() make it known again. An unknown register read back at its power-up value is taken as a reset, DeviceReset ; any other value is adopted. When the failed write's old or new value was itself the power-up value, that is a false DeviceReset : one time, nothing written, and EnsureInitialized() recovers. After a failed ApplyConfig() the registers written before the failure hold the new values, the one that failed is unknown, and the rest keep the old ones. GetConfig() is the driver's copy, so after a failed write it shows the riskier value for the direction, the drive strength and 0x4F, and the written level for the outputs: not necessarily what the pins do. Read the chip with ReadOutputLatch() (and ReadInputMask() ) when it matters. One pin call, and what each outcome leaves Figure description and sources Top to bottom on the left, the steps of SetOutputs(); the other pin setters take the same path to their own register pair. The call first checks that the driver is started and the mask is not 0, with no I/O. It computes the new output pair from the driver's copy (GetConfig()) without reading the chip, and writes it in one transfer. With Verify::ReadBack passed (the default is Verify::None) it reads the pair back. The cards on the right are the outcomes: Bus may have delivered the pair, so the copy takes the written level, marked unknown, and the next call reads it before building on it; WriteMismatch means the chip acknowledged the write but holds something else, and the copy keeps what was asked, so retrying the call sends it again; Ok updates the copy. The band at the bottom contrasts the copy with ReadOutputLatch(), which reads the output pair from the chip, and says how a handler retries. EnsureInitialized (); // first call starts the chip; then Ok, no I/O if ( ! r ) { std :: printf ( "PCAL9555A start: %s \n " , pcal9555 :: ToString ( r . error )); // the next call retries } return r . error ; } The constructor stores the port, the address and the configuration and does no I/O. EnsureInitialized() is the one way to start the chip. Its first call checks the configuration ( Validate() ) and the address, brings the bus up, reads the input ports to see that a part ACKs, on a PCAL9555A reads 0x4F and checks that its reserved bits are 0, then writes every register of the configuration and reads each back. A register that does not hold what was written means another part answers at the address: DeviceIdMismatch . Once it has succeeded, EnsureInitialized() returns Ok at once with no I/O, so a caller (or a handler that owns the driver) can call it before every use. After a failure the driver stays uninitialised and the next call starts again from the beginning. No other call starts the chip: before EnsureInitialized() succeeds every read and write returns NotInitialized and sends nothing. ApplyConfig() before the start only stores the configuration for the first EnsureInitialized() . The chip has no reset, so the start-up writes every register instead: the result is the same whatever the chip held before, a power-up or a previous run of the firmware.

The output latch is kept for input pins, so it can be prepared while the pin is still an input. SetDirection() is the one pin call that sends more than its own register. A pin that becomes an output drives its latch through its port's output stage, and a power-on reset sets every latch high and every stage push-pull (table 4). So it first checks for a reset (one read, see Recover after a power loss ), then writes from the driver's copy in the data sheet's order (section 6.2.12): 0x4F on a PCAL9555A, the output pair, the configuration pair. Whatever the chip went through, no pin becomes an output at a level or stage you did not set. It costs one read and two write pairs on a PCA9555, plus a 1-byte write on a PCAL9555A (about 0.3 ms at 400 kHz instead of 90 µs); call it at configuration time, not in a fast loop. Releasing pins ( Direction::Input ) is the safe direction, and the cheapest. When every pin ends up an input, the configuration pair is the only transfer: no check, nothing before it that could fail, since nothing can be driven whatever the chip went through. When other pins stay outputs, the reset check comes first, then the configuration pair, so the pins are released by the first write, then 0x4F and the output pair for the remaining outputs. The driver keeps a copy of every register it wrote ( GetConfig() ), computes the new pair from it and writes the pair in one transfer, without reading it first: by default a pin call other than SetDirection() is the one 3-byte write the data sheet needs and nothing more. Read-back is chosen per call: every setter takes a last argument Verify , Verify::None by default. With Verify::ReadBack the call then reads the pair back, a 2-byte read that more than doubles its bus time, and a write the chip acknowledged but did not keep returns Error::WriteMismatch . An acknowledge carries no checksum, and the data sheet allows for a glitch or data corruption (section 8.3); the output port reads back the value it holds, not the pin (section 6.2.3), so the read-back shows what the chip will drive. Pass Verify::ReadBack on the calls where a lost write matters more than the bus time, such as a driver enable, and leave the hot path at the default. A write whose transfer failed ( Bus , NoDevice ) may still have reached the chip: the bytes can be stored before a lost ACK or a NACK of the last byte. So after a failed write the copy does not keep the old value as if nothing happened. It takes the riskier of the old and the asked value, and the register is marked unknown: Register pair The copy after a failed write Configuration ( input_mask ) A pin that was or was asked to be an output counts as an output (old AND asked) Output port ( output_high_mask ) The written level Drive strength ( drive_strength_codes ) The stronger code of each pin 0x4F ( port0_mode , port1_mode ) Push-pull if either was push-pull Polarity, input latch, pull enable and selection, interrupt mask The written value The next call that builds on an unknown register first reads it from the chip into the copy (one more read, only after a failure), so it never computes a new value from a stale one; a successful write of the pair, a read-back call ( ReadOutputLatch() , ReadInputMask() , ReadPolarityInversion() ), ApplyConfig() and EnsureInitialized() make it known again. An unknown register read back at its power-up value is taken as a reset, DeviceReset ; any other value is adopted. When the failed write's old or new value was itself the power-up value, that is a false DeviceReset : one time, nothing written, and EnsureInitialized() recovers. After a failed ApplyConfig() the registers written before the failure hold the new values, the one that failed is unknown, and the rest keep the old ones. GetConfig() is the driver's copy, so after a failed write it shows the riskier value for the direction, the drive strength and 0x4F, and the written level for the outputs: not necessarily what the pins do. Read the chip with ReadOutputLatch() (and ReadInputMask() ) when it matters. One pin call, and what each outcome leaves Figure description and sources Top to bottom on the left, the steps of SetOutputs(); the other pin setters take the same path to their own register pair. The call first checks that the driver is started and the mask is not 0, with no I/O. It computes the new output pair from the driver's copy (GetConfig()) without reading the chip, and writes it in one transfer. With Verify::ReadBack passed (the default is Verify::None) it reads the pair back. The cards on the right are the outcomes: Bus may have delivered the pair, so the copy takes the written level, marked unknown, and the next call reads it before building on it; WriteMismatch means the chip acknowledged the write but holds something else, and the copy keeps what was asked, so retrying the call sends it again; Ok updates the copy. The band at the bottom contrasts the copy with ReadOutputLatch(), which reads the output pair from the chip, and says how a handler retries. A write to the checked register that the chip acknowledged but dropped reads the same way; the recovery is the same. If a call returns Bus or NoDevice , start again too: Deinitialize() (a failing write still leaves the driver uninitialised), then EnsureInitialized() , which writes every register from the driver's copy. The ESP32 example does both.

docs.text: On a board, the driver usually sits under a handler that owns it, the port and the bus, and that hands pins to the rest of the firmware. The driver leaves to the handler what it cannot know: Start-up. The handler calls EnsureInitialized() from its own lazy start; the driver never starts itself, so a read before it returns NotInitialized instead of doing hidden I/O on a time-critical path. Retries. The driver never retries. On WriteMismatch or Bus from a pin call, retry the call a bounded number of times and count the attempts (handbook KB-ARCH-044); the driver stays started. Every pin call writes a whole register pair from the copy, so repeating it is safe. On NoDevice do not retry the call: the chip is gone or unpowered, so recover as below. After WriteMismatch the copy holds what was asked for, so an absolute call ( SetOutputs() , WriteOutputs() , SetDirection() , ...) can simply be repeated; a relative one, ToggleOutputs() , cannot (it would toggle back): resend with WriteOutputs(GetConfig().output_high_mask) . Recovery. If the bus needs a reset (clocking SCL free, re-initialising the peripheral), do it in the port or the handler, then Deinitialize() and EnsureInitialized() : every register is written again from the copy. Locks and threads. The driver takes no lock; the handler serialises the calls, and the bus lock belongs in the port. Time. Every call is at most 24 transfers and never waits, so its duration is the port's: give the port a short timeout (a few milliseconds at 100 kHz), and keep expander calls off threads with hard deadlines: a long I2C timeout on a time-critical thread stalls it for that long whenever the bus fails. The part. Choose Config::variant from the board: a PCAL9555A configured as a PCA9555 works, without the Agile I/O calls; the reverse fails at start-up with DeviceIdMismatch .

docs.text: const char * Describe ( pcal9555 :: Error e ) { switch ( e ) { case pcal9555 :: Error :: NoDevice : return "nothing acknowledges the address: check the address pins and the supply" ; case pcal9555 :: Error :: Bus : return "a transfer failed: check the pull-ups, the bus length and the supply" ; case pcal9555 :: Error :: DeviceIdMismatch : return "another part answers at this address, or the variant is wrong" ; case pcal9555 :: Error :: DeviceReset : return "the expander reset (supply dip): call EnsureInitialized() again" ; case pcal9555 :: Error :: Unsupported : return "an Agile I/O feature on a PCA9555: set Config::variant if a PCAL9555A is fitted" ; default : return pcal9555 :: ToString ( e ); } } Signal Meaning What to do Error::NoDevice Nothing acknowledged the address (only with a port that has GetLastFailure() ) Check the address pins and the supply; Deinitialize() , then EnsureInitialized() Error::Bus The port failed a transfer or the bus bring-up: a bus error, a refused command byte, or, with a port without GetLastFailure() , also an absent chip Check the pull-ups, the bus and the supply (and the address pins); Deinitialize() , then EnsureInitialized() Error::DeviceIdMismatch At start-up, a register did not read back what was written, or a reserved bit of 0x4F read 1 Another part at the address, or variant set to Pcal9555a on a PCA9555 Error::DeviceReset A running driver found a register back at its power-up value: the chip went through a power-on reset (or dropped a write to that register). Nothing was written; the driver is uninitialised EnsureInitialized() , which writes the copy again in order; if it repeats, check the expander's supply Error::WriteMismatch After the start, a register did not keep what a call just wrote Retry the same call (it resends what GetConfig() holds); if it repeats, check the bus (pull-ups, length, noise) and ReadOutputLatch() Error::Unsupported An Agile I/O call or Config field on a driver configured for the PCA9555 Set Config::variant to Pcal9555a if a PCAL9555A is fitted Error::InvalidArgument A mask of 0, a pin above 15, an address outside 0x20 to 0x27, a value that is not an enumerator, or a changed variant; nothing was sent Fix the value ( Validate() ) Error::NotInitialized EnsureInitialized() has not succeeded, or a call returned DeviceReset Call it Error::Timeout , Error::Crc , Error::Busy and Error::DeviceFault belong to the shared base set but are never returned by this driver: the chip has no timed operation, no CRC, no busy state and no fault flag. Every value, with the calls that return it, is on the Contract page. pcal9555::ToString() names an error for a log. Next: Agile I/O .

The layers, one of them yours Figure description and sources Top to bottom, each arrow is a call. Your application calls one object, whose public calls are listed from the umbrella header in inc/. The core turns each call into register reads and writes and hands them to the port contract (the CRTP base in inc/*_interface.hpp), which forwards them, at compile time, to the hooks of the port class you write; your port moves the bytes on the bus. The chip has no conversion or reset time, so the port has no delay hook and every call is a fixed number of transfers. One error type. Result<T> carries a value and an Error ; nothing throws and nothing returns a bare bool . No heap, no exceptions, no RTTI, no std::function , no printf . docs.text: Changelog ¶ What changed in each release of the driver. Entries under Breaking need source changes in code that used the affected API. [Unreleased] ¶ Changed ¶ The repository moved to kokeb-labs-drivers; URLs follow. Hardware page: the pinout, the block diagram and the application circuit are now figures drawn from docs/hardware.yml , which also generates the pin table (replacing the hand-written one) and the parts table. Every pin, block and part cites the datasheet section and page; values the datasheet does not give are marked as not confirmed. kokeb-docs hardware --kicad-netlist exports the circuit. Synced with the driver template: tools/preflight.sh runs clang-tidy over every file CI lints, as CI does, and the hardware-lessons review adds the switch-off, channel-in-doubt and fuzz-skip lessons. [0.1.0] - 2026-11-09 ¶ Breaking ¶ Error::DeviceReset (18) is new. A switch over Error without default: must add it ( -Wswitch ). SetDirection() and ApplyConfig() now return it, and so does a setter about to rewrite the register the reset check reads, when the expander went through a power-on reset since the start; the driver is then uninitialised, so call EnsureInitialized() again. Since v0.1.0-rc.1: Config::verify_writes is removed. Read-back is now chosen per call: every pin and Agile I/O setter ( SetDirection() , SetOutputs() , WriteOutputs() , ToggleOutputs() , SetPolarityInversion() , SetDriveStrength() , SetPull() , SetInputLatch() , SetInterruptEnabled() , SetOutputMode() ) takes a last argument Verify verify = Verify::None , a new enum in pcal9555_types.hpp . Code that set verify_writes = false drops that line; code that wants the read-back passes Verify::ReadBack to the calls that need it. A value that is not an enumerator returns InvalidArgument with no I/O. Error is enum class [[nodiscard]] Error : a call whose Error is dropped (for example Validate(config); as a statement) now warns, and fails a -Werror build. Use the value, or cast it to void on purpose. Error::NoDevice (17) is new. A switch over Error without default: must add it ( -Wswitch ). It is returned only with a port that has the new optional GetLastFailure() hook; a port without it sees Bus as before. GetConfig() on a temporary driver (an rvalue) is deleted, since the reference it returned would dangle; call it on a named driver. reg::kDriveBitsPerPin is a uint32_t (was uint8_t ). The port hooks keep their signatures: EnsureInitialized() , Write() and WriteRead() are unchanged, and the new hook is optional, so an existing port compiles as it is. A port whose hooks were not noexcept , or took another length type than std::size_t , no longer satisfies I2cPort (it broke the documented contract before). Added ¶ CheckForReset() : finds a power-on reset (section 6.4) by reading one register whose copy differs from its power-up value; one read, none when the copy is all power-up values, plus one per register whose last write failed when no other register is left to read. The bus requirements as constexpr values in pcal9555_i2c_interface.hpp , with their data sheet sections: kI2cAddress (0x20, section 6.1), kMaxClockHz (400 kHz, section 13 table 33) and kRepeatedStart (section 7.2). The host and ESP32 example ports check their clock, their address and the repeated START against them with static_assert . kDefaultI2cAddress stays, with the same value. The optional port hook bool GetLastFailure(I2cFailure& failure) noexcept and enum class I2cFailure ( Other , AddressNack , DataNack ). When a transfer fails and the port reports AddressNack , every call returns Error::NoDevice instead of Bus , so an absent or unpowered chip is told apart from a bus fault. The host example port implements it; the ESP32 port does not, because i2c_master does not say which byte was NACKed. Raw access and diagnostics: ReadRegister(command) (one read, no retry, any command byte the configured part implements, reg::IsImplemented() ), GetLastInputs() , GetLastOutput() and an interrupt latch, GetLatchedInterrupts() and ClearLatchedInterrupts() , which keeps every interrupt status the driver read after the input read that clears it. None of the accessors does I/O, and the hot path gains two compares per read and no transfer. Config::operator== (every field is an integer or an enumeration). Tests: a model independent of the driver's headers, with its own register map and data sheet sections, and tests/test_model.cpp , which compares the two maps at compile time; bus line modes (SDA floating or stuck low) and a deaf device against the start-up and every read; NoDevice with and without the hook; compile-fail tests for a narrowed hook parameter, a hook without noexcept and misdeclared optional hooks. The fuzzer also chooses address NACKs and whether the port can tell them, and checks that NoDevice appears only after one. Strict-dialect header checks ( pcal9555_header_checks ): every public header compiled alone as ISO C++20 with -pedantic-errors on GCC and Clang, in the Cortex-M cross-build, and in the ESP-IDF build through examples/esp32/main/pcal9555_cxx20_check.cpp . The review skills cpp20-profile , misra-review and hardware-lessons-review , and a read-only reviewer definition, from the driver template. First version of the driver for the NXP PCA9555 and PCAL9555A 16-bit I2C GPIO expanders, written on the Kokeb Labs driver template. pcal9555::PCAL9555<Port> with the configuration in the constructor and one start-up call, EnsureInitialized() : presence check by reading the input ports, every register written and read back as the identity check, and on a PCAL9555A the reserved bits of 0x4F checked before any write. ApplyConfig() , Deinitialize() (every pin an input). Pin calls by mask, each one register-pair transfer from the driver's copy of the registers: SetDirection() , SetOutputs() , WriteOutputs() , ToggleOutputs() , SetPolarityInversion() , ReadInputs() , ReadPin() . PCAL9555A Agile I/O: SetDriveStrength() , SetPull() , SetInputLatch() , SetInterruptEnabled() , ReadInterruptStatus() , SetOutputMode() ; Config::variant selects the part and the Agile I/O calls return Unsupported on a PCA9555. Config with the power-up value of every register, a constexpr Validate() , PinMask() , AddressFromPins() and DriveStrengthAll() ; Kconfig options for the variant, the output levels and the directions. Host tests over a protocol model of both parts, with every transfer of every operation failed in turn; the host and ESP32 examples. Not verified on hardware. clang-tidy runs the CERT C++ checks ( cert-* ) as well; the library code had no finding. The Log() hook is documented as void Log(LogLevel, const char* message) : the message is plain text, and the examples print it with "%s" instead of using it as a format string (no C variadic function, CERT DCL50-CPP; no format string from data). A port with the old variadic signature still compiles. After WriteMismatch every setter's copy holds what was asked for, SetDriveStrength() included; retry an absolute call as it was, and after ToggleOutputs() resend with WriteOutputs(GetConfig().output_high_mask) (a repeated toggle would undo it). ReadOutputLatch() , ReadInputMask() and ReadPolarityInversion() read what the chip holds, not the driver's copy; the Output Port registers read back the output latch, not the pin, so a lost write shows there. Config::verify_writes (default on): once started, every write is read back, and a register that did not keep its value returns Error::WriteMismatch (16), the driver's first chip-specific error. An I2C acknowledge carries no checksum, and the data sheet allows for data corruption (PCAL9555A section 8.3). A register that does not keep its value after the start is WriteMismatch ; DeviceIdMismatch now means only "another part answers", at start-up. Three chip figures drawn from the source: the register map with each pair's owner and power-up value (Hardware), what one pin call does with verify_writes and how a handler retries (API guide), and the EnsureInitialized() steps with the error each one returns (Contract). A libFuzzer target over failed, lost and replaced transfers ( tests/fuzz/ , -DPCAL9555_BUILD_FUZZERS=ON ); its corpus replays as a CTest on every compiler, and CI fuzzes every pull request. API guide: "Read back what the chip holds" and "Use it from a handler" (start-up, retries, recovery, locks, timeouts). docs/datasheets.yml (handbook ADR-0019): the PCAL9555A (Rev. 2) and PCA9555 (Rev. 10) data sheets with their SHA-256, and every topic the driver takes from them. kokeb-docs gen builds from it the README card, the Datasheet map page ( docs/datasheet.md ) and a box of the sections each page relies on. The README is restructured as the front door: at a glance, wiring, port, first code, what it does, and which page to read for what. Documentation site with the Doxygen API reference: https://kokeb-labs-drivers.github.io/driver-pcal9555/ . Releases carry a source archive, an SPDX SBOM, one zip per example firmware build, SHA256SUMS , and signed build provenance for every file (check a download with gh attestation verify ). Changed ¶ The misra-review , cpp20-profile and new-driver-from-template skills and docs/repo-setup.md follow the template: reading the MISRA report, the known tool misfires, enumeration ranges without a sentinel, and the settings tool. tools/preflight.sh and the verify and hardware-lessons-review skills follow the template: every check CI runs that a workstation can run, in one command, and the rules for device resets, faults the chip clears itself, dropped writes, switch-offs that no uncertainty refuses and a model that changes state on its own. Follows the driver template's portable ownership: copyright belongs to The driver-pcal9555 authors ( LICENSE , every source header, driver.yml authors , the docs footer). tools/check_standalone.py runs in the Handbook source checks job and keeps the code and docs about this chip only. AGENTS.md follows the template's structure; the issue and PR templates ask for the board, MCU and port in one field. The port concepts match each hook's address against exactly one noexcept signature with detail::ExactHook<Port, Sig>::Take(&Port::Hook) instead of probing it with a converting detail::Exactly<T> : no conversion operator is left. A misdeclared hook is still a compile error. kAlwaysFalse takes a class and the enumeration helpers an enumeration ( ClassType , Enumeration ), each with a compile-fail test. HasGetLastFailure matches bool GetLastFailure(I2cFailure&) noexcept the same way. Both datasheets are listed with the kind Datasheet , so the generated cards and the Datasheet map name the datasheet on every line that carries its revision date. Include guards ( #ifndef PCAL9555_..._HPP ) replace #pragma once in every header, the .ipp and the test and example headers. Every target builds as ISO C++20 ( CMAKE_CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF , -pedantic-errors , the C++20 deprecation warnings as errors), the tests and fuzzers with the standard library's bounds checks. The port concept checks the hooks exactly: each argument's type, noexcept and the bool result. The optional hooks are detected by named concepts in one place, and one declared with another signature is a compile error. Narrow operands are widened to uint32_t before every shift and bitwise operation, enumerations are checked with one helper before use, and the bus helpers take spans with the size fixed at compile time; a zero-length transfer is refused before any I/O. Validate() compares the whole Config with its power-up value for a PCA9555, so an Agile I/O field added later is covered without a change there. Behaviour change: the start-up identity check writes reg::kIdentityPattern (0x55AA) to the polarity inversion pair and reads it back before any configured value is written (two more transfers; at most 24 for a PCAL9555A start-up). A floating or stuck line, or a device that acknowledges everything and reads a fixed byte, now fails with DeviceIdMismatch whatever the Config ; before, a Config whose registers matched that byte passed. The polarity pair changes only how inputs read, so no pin is driven before the identity is confirmed. A first drive strength pair that reads back differently no longer marks pins 8 to 15 as changed in GetConfig() : their pair was never sent. An optional hook declared with any other parameter list ( GetLastFailure() with no argument or an rvalue reference, Log() without the level) is a compile error instead of being ignored. Deinitialize() clears GetLastInputs() , GetLastOutput() and the interrupt latch. The presence check's input read is documented as clearing an interrupt left pending from before the start. The documentation describes only this driver against its data sheets: the Status page explains each design choice (read-back on request, the identity pattern, outputs before directions, no waits) by data sheet section, and the API guide, Testing and Porting pages give bench steps as procedures. The source checks job runs the handbook's checks/source_checks.py at its C++20-profile commit; the managed files (skills, _config/.clang-tidy , ci-repo-checks.yml ) follow driver template a4a1056. CI runs fewer jobs, from the driver template: the host tests build GCC and Clang in one job; DCO, the org standard, Markdown and YAML lint, the handbook rules, template drift and cppcheck are steps of one Repository checks job ( ci-repo-checks.yml , replacing ci-handbook.yml , ci-cpp-analysis.yml , ci-markdown-lint.yml and ci-yaml-lint.yml ); cross-compile and host quality use ci-tools' one-job layouts. No check is dropped. The workflows have no manual ( workflow_dispatch ) trigger any more. Behaviour change: a pin call no longer reads its write back by default (it did with the old verify_writes , which defaulted to on). A timing-critical call now makes only the transfer the data sheet needs, and a write the chip acknowledged but lost is no longer reported unless the call passes Verify::ReadBack , which costs one more I2C read per register written and returns WriteMismatch on a difference. EnsureInitialized() and ApplyConfig() still read every register back, unconditionally. The README and the Testing page link to the handbook, which is now public. MISRA C++:2023 conformance: parentheses make operator precedence explicit (Rule 8.0.1); the compile-time test vectors pass arguments of the parameter's exact type through the new detail literals _u8 , _u16 and _u32 , which do not compile for a value out of range (Rule 7.0.6); every if ... else if chain ends with an else (Rule 9.4.1); ToString(Error) ends its switch with default: and the host tests build with -Wswitch-enum , so a new enumerator still warns (Rule 9.4.2); the register write loop has a constant bound (Rule 9.5.1); the private writeAll() and verifyAll() declarations use the definitions' parameter names (Rule 13.3.3); Config::operator== is a [[nodiscard]] hidden friend (Rule 16.6.1); and the .ipp include at the end of pcal9555.hpp carries the deviation marker MD-CPP-009 (Rule 19.0.3). Behaviour is unchanged. Fixed ¶ After a power-on reset of the expander, SetDirection() on any pin turned the old outputs back on, high and push-pull (table 4), and Verify::ReadBack passed: it wrote only the configuration pair. It now checks for a reset first ( DeviceReset , nothing written) and writes 0x4F, the output pair and the configuration pair from the copy, in the data sheet's order (section 6.2.12). Cost: one read plus one write pair on a PCA9555, plus a 1-byte write on a PCAL9555A. On a PCAL9555A with an unmasked input, ReadInputs() and ReadPin() cleared the interrupt status before the interrupt latch saw it (sections 6.2.11, 6.5). They now read the status pair into GetLatchedInterrupts() first: one more read per input read while an input is unmasked. A write whose transfer failed with Bus could still have reached the chip (a NACK or a lost ACK after the bytes), but the copy kept the old value and later setters built on it: a failed SetDirection(..., Input) left the pin an output while the copy said input, and a following ToggleOutputs() inverted a stale level. The copy now takes the riskier of the old and the asked value (configuration: output if either; output port: the written level; drive strength: the stronger code; 0x4F: push-pull if either; the other pairs: the written value), the register is marked unknown, and the next call that builds on it reads it first (one more read, only after a failure). A successful write of the pair, ReadOutputLatch() , ReadInputMask() , ReadPolarityInversion() , ApplyConfig() and EnsureInitialized() make it known again; the reset check never reads an unknown register. NoDevice (an address NACK) leaves the copy unchanged. An unknown register read back at its power-up value is DeviceReset (falsely, once, when the failed write's old or new value was the power-up value); with no other register to check, the reset check reads the unknown ones. A failed ApplyConfig() now leaves the new values of the registers written before the failure, the failed one unknown and the rest at their old values, instead of the previous configuration. SetDirection(..., Direction::Input) that leaves every pin an input writes only the configuration pair, with no reset check; releasing while other outputs remain writes the configuration pair before 0x4F and the output pair, so a failure after it leaves the pins released. The chip model can go through a power-on reset on its own in the middle of a session ( reset_after ), and the fuzzer chooses resets between calls.

docs.text: Error::DeviceReset (18) is new. A switch over Error without default: must add it ( -Wswitch ). SetDirection() and ApplyConfig() now return it, and so does a setter about to rewrite the register the reset check reads, when the expander went through a power-on reset since the start; the driver is then uninitialised, so call EnsureInitialized() again. Since v0.1.0-rc.1: Config::verify_writes is removed. Read-back is now chosen per call: every pin and Agile I/O setter ( SetDirection() , SetOutputs() , WriteOutputs() , ToggleOutputs() , SetPolarityInversion() , SetDriveStrength() , SetPull() , SetInputLatch() , SetInterruptEnabled() , SetOutputMode() ) takes a last argument Verify verify = Verify::None , a new enum in pcal9555_types.hpp . Code that set verify_writes = false drops that line; code that wants the read-back passes Verify::ReadBack to the calls that need it. A value that is not an enumerator returns InvalidArgument with no I/O. Error is enum class [[nodiscard]] Error : a call whose Error is dropped (for example Validate(config); as a statement) now warns, and fails a -Werror build. Use the value, or cast it to void on purpose. Error::NoDevice (17) is new. A switch over Error without default: must add it ( -Wswitch ). It is returned only with a port that has the new optional GetLastFailure() hook; a port without it sees Bus as before. GetConfig() on a temporary driver (an rvalue) is deleted, since the reference it returned would dangle; call it on a named driver. reg::kDriveBitsPerPin is a uint32_t (was uint8_t ). The port hooks keep their signatures: EnsureInitialized() , Write() and WriteRead() are unchanged, and the new hook is optional, so an existing port compiles as it is. A port whose hooks were not noexcept , or took another length type than std::size_t , no longer satisfies I2cPort (it broke the documented contract before).

docs.text: CheckForReset() : finds a power-on reset (section 6.4) by reading one register whose copy differs from its power-up value; one read, none when the copy is all power-up values, plus one per register whose last write failed when no other register is left to read. The bus requirements as constexpr values in pcal9555_i2c_interface.hpp , with their data sheet sections: kI2cAddress (0x20, section 6.1), kMaxClockHz (400 kHz, section 13 table 33) and kRepeatedStart (section 7.2). The host and ESP32 example ports check their clock, their address and the repeated START against them with static_assert . kDefaultI2cAddress stays, with the same value. The optional port hook bool GetLastFailure(I2cFailure& failure) noexcept and enum class I2cFailure ( Other , AddressNack , DataNack ). When a transfer fails and the port reports AddressNack , every call returns Error::NoDevice instead of Bus , so an absent or unpowered chip is told apart from a bus fault. The host example port implements it; the ESP32 port does not, because i2c_master does not say which byte was NACKed. Raw access and diagnostics: ReadRegister(command) (one read, no retry, any command byte the configured part implements, reg::IsImplemented() ), GetLastInputs() , GetLastOutput() and an interrupt latch, GetLatchedInterrupts() and ClearLatchedInterrupts() , which keeps every interrupt status the driver read after the input read that clears it. None of the accessors does I/O, and the hot path gains two compares per read and no transfer. Config::operator== (every field is an integer or an enumeration). Tests: a model independent of the driver's headers, with its own register map and data sheet sections, and tests/test_model.cpp , which compares the two maps at compile time; bus line modes (SDA floating or stuck low) and a deaf device against the start-up and every read; NoDevice with and without the hook; compile-fail tests for a narrowed hook parameter, a hook without noexcept and misdeclared optional hooks. The fuzzer also chooses address NACKs and whether the port can tell them, and checks that NoDevice appears only after one. Strict-dialect header checks ( pcal9555_header_checks ): every public header compiled alone as ISO C++20 with -pedantic-errors on GCC and Clang, in the Cortex-M cross-build, and in the ESP-IDF build through examples/esp32/main/pcal9555_cxx20_check.cpp . The review skills cpp20-profile , misra-review and hardware-lessons-review , and a read-only reviewer definition, from the driver template. First version of the driver for the NXP PCA9555 and PCAL9555A 16-bit I2C GPIO expanders, written on the Kokeb Labs driver template. pcal9555::PCAL9555<Port> with the configuration in the constructor and one start-up call, EnsureInitialized() : presence check by reading the input ports, every register written and read back as the identity check, and on a PCAL9555A the reserved bits of 0x4F checked before any write. ApplyConfig() , Deinitialize() (every pin an input). Pin calls by mask, each one register-pair transfer from the driver's copy of the registers: SetDirection() , SetOutputs() , WriteOutputs() , ToggleOutputs() , SetPolarityInversion() , ReadInputs() , ReadPin() . PCAL9555A Agile I/O: SetDriveStrength() , SetPull() , SetInputLatch() , SetInterruptEnabled() , ReadInterruptStatus() , SetOutputMode() ; Config::variant selects the part and the Agile I/O calls return Unsupported on a PCA9555. Config with the power-up value of every register, a constexpr Validate() , PinMask() , AddressFromPins() and DriveStrengthAll() ; Kconfig options for the variant, the output levels and the directions. Host tests over a protocol model of both parts, with every transfer of every operation failed in turn; the host and ESP32 examples. Not verified on hardware. clang-tidy runs the CERT C++ checks ( cert-* ) as well; the library code had no finding. The Log() hook is documented as void Log(LogLevel, const char* message) : the message is plain text, and the examples print it with "%s" instead of using it as a format string (no C variadic function, CERT DCL50-CPP; no format string from data). A port with the old variadic signature still compiles. After WriteMismatch every setter's copy holds what was asked for, SetDriveStrength() included; retry an absolute call as it was, and after ToggleOutputs() resend with WriteOutputs(GetConfig().output_high_mask) (a repeated toggle would undo it). ReadOutputLatch() , ReadInputMask() and ReadPolarityInversion() read what the chip holds, not the driver's copy; the Output Port registers read back the output latch, not the pin, so a lost write shows there. Config::verify_writes (default on): once started, every write is read back, and a register that did not keep its value returns Error::WriteMismatch (16), the driver's first chip-specific error. An I2C acknowledge carries no checksum, and the data sheet allows for data corruption (PCAL9555A section 8.3). A register that does not keep its value after the start is WriteMismatch ; DeviceIdMismatch now means only "another part answers", at start-up. Three chip figures drawn from the source: the register map with each pair's owner and power-up value (Hardware), what one pin call does with verify_writes and how a handler retries (API guide), and the EnsureInitialized() steps with the error each one returns (Contract). A libFuzzer target over failed, lost and replaced transfers ( tests/fuzz/ , -DPCAL9555_BUILD_FUZZERS=ON ); its corpus replays as a CTest on every compiler, and CI fuzzes every pull request. API guide: "Read back what the chip holds" and "Use it from a handler" (start-up, retries, recovery, locks, timeouts). docs/datasheets.yml (handbook ADR-0019): the PCAL9555A (Rev. 2) and PCA9555 (Rev. 10) data sheets with their SHA-256, and every topic the driver takes from them. kokeb-docs gen builds from it the README card, the Datasheet map page ( docs/datasheet.md ) and a box of the sections each page relies on. The README is restructured as the front door: at a glance, wiring, port, first code, what it does, and which page to read for what. Documentation site with the Doxygen API reference: https://kokeb-labs-drivers.github.io/driver-pcal9555/ . Releases carry a source archive, an SPDX SBOM, one zip per example firmware build, SHA256SUMS , and signed build provenance for every file (check a download with gh attestation verify ).

docs.text: The misra-review , cpp20-profile and new-driver-from-template skills and docs/repo-setup.md follow the template: reading the MISRA report, the known tool misfires, enumeration ranges without a sentinel, and the settings tool. tools/preflight.sh and the verify and hardware-lessons-review skills follow the template: every check CI runs that a workstation can run, in one command, and the rules for device resets, faults the chip clears itself, dropped writes, switch-offs that no uncertainty refuses and a model that changes state on its own. Follows the driver template's portable ownership: copyright belongs to The driver-pcal9555 authors ( LICENSE , every source header, driver.yml authors , the docs footer). tools/check_standalone.py runs in the Handbook source checks job and keeps the code and docs about this chip only. AGENTS.md follows the template's structure; the issue and PR templates ask for the board, MCU and port in one field. The port concepts match each hook's address against exactly one noexcept signature with detail::ExactHook<Port, Sig>::Take(&Port::Hook) instead of probing it with a converting detail::Exactly<T> : no conversion operator is left. A misdeclared hook is still a compile error. kAlwaysFalse takes a class and the enumeration helpers an enumeration ( ClassType , Enumeration ), each with a compile-fail test. HasGetLastFailure matches bool GetLastFailure(I2cFailure&) noexcept the same way. Both datasheets are listed with the kind Datasheet , so the generated cards and the Datasheet map name the datasheet on every line that carries its revision date. Include guards ( #ifndef PCAL9555_..._HPP ) replace #pragma once in every header, the .ipp and the test and example headers. Every target builds as ISO C++20 ( CMAKE_CXX_EXTENSIONS OFF , -pedantic-errors , the C++20 deprecation warnings as errors), the tests and fuzzers with the standard library's bounds checks. The port concept checks the hooks exactly: each argument's type, noexcept and the bool result. The optional hooks are detected by named concepts in one place, and one declared with another signature is a compile error. Narrow operands are widened to uint32_t before every shift and bitwise operation, enumerations are checked with one helper before use, and the bus helpers take spans with the size fixed at compile time; a zero-length transfer is refused before any I/O. Validate() compares the whole Config with its power-up value for a PCA9555, so an Agile I/O field added later is covered without a change there. Behaviour change: the start-up identity check writes reg::kIdentityPattern (0x55AA) to the polarity inversion pair and reads it back before any configured value is written (two more transfers; at most 24 for a PCAL9555A start-up). A floating or stuck line, or a device that acknowledges everything and reads a fixed byte, now fails with DeviceIdMismatch whatever the Config ; before, a Config whose registers matched that byte passed. The polarity pair changes only how inputs read, so no pin is driven before the identity is confirmed. A first drive strength pair that reads back differently no longer marks pins 8 to 15 as changed in GetConfig() : their pair was never sent. An optional hook declared with any other parameter list ( GetLastFailure() with no argument or an rvalue reference, Log() without the level) is a compile error instead of being ignored. Deinitialize() clears GetLastInputs() , GetLastOutput() and the interrupt latch. The presence check's input read is documented as clearing an interrupt left pending from before the start. The documentation describes only this driver against its data sheets: the Status page explains each design choice (read-back on request, the identity pattern, outputs before directions, no waits) by data sheet section, and the API guide, Testing and Porting pages give bench steps as procedures. The source checks job runs the handbook's checks/source_checks.py at its C++20-profile commit; the managed files (skills, _config/.clang-tidy , ci-repo-checks.yml ) follow driver template a4a1056. CI runs fewer jobs, from the driver template: the host tests build GCC and Clang in one job; DCO, the org standard, Markdown and YAML lint, the handbook rules, template drift and cppcheck are steps of one Repository checks job ( ci-repo-checks.yml , replacing ci-handbook.yml , ci-cpp-analysis.yml , ci-markdown-lint.yml and ci-yaml-lint.yml ); cross-compile and host quality use ci-tools' one-job layouts. No check is dropped. The workflows have no manual ( workflow_dispatch ) trigger any more. Behaviour change: a pin call no longer reads its write back by default (it did with the old verify_writes , which defaulted to on). A timing-critical call now makes only the transfer the data sheet needs, and a write the chip acknowledged but lost is no longer reported unless the call passes Verify::ReadBack , which costs one more I2C read per register written and returns WriteMismatch on a difference. EnsureInitialized() and ApplyConfig() still read every register back, unconditionally. The README and the Testing page link to the handbook, which is now public. MISRA C++:2023 conformance: parentheses make operator precedence explicit (Rule 8.0.1); the compile-time test vectors pass arguments of the parameter's exact type through the new detail literals _u8 , _u16 and _u32 , which do not compile for a value out of range (Rule 7.0.6); every if ... else if chain ends with an else (Rule 9.4.1); ToString(Error) ends its switch with default: and the host tests build with -Wswitch-enum , so a new enumerator still warns (Rule 9.4.2); the register write loop has a constant bound (Rule 9.5.1); the private writeAll() and verifyAll() declarations use the definitions' parameter names (Rule 13.3.3); Config::operator== is a [[nodiscard]] hidden friend (Rule 16.6.1); and the .ipp include at the end of pcal9555.hpp carries the deviation marker MD-CPP-009 (Rule 19.0.3). Behaviour is unchanged.

docs.text: After a power-on reset of the expander, SetDirection() on any pin turned the old outputs back on, high and push-pull (table 4), and Verify::ReadBack passed: it wrote only the configuration pair. It now checks for a reset first ( DeviceReset , nothing written) and writes 0x4F, the output pair and the configuration pair from the copy, in the data sheet's order (section 6.2.12). Cost: one read plus one write pair on a PCA9555, plus a 1-byte write on a PCAL9555A. On a PCAL9555A with an unmasked input, ReadInputs() and ReadPin() cleared the interrupt status before the interrupt latch saw it (sections 6.2.11, 6.5). They now read the status pair into GetLatchedInterrupts() first: one more read per input read while an input is unmasked. A write whose transfer failed with Bus could still have reached the chip (a NACK or a lost ACK after the bytes), but the copy kept the old value and later setters built on it: a failed SetDirection(..., Input) left the pin an output while the copy said input, and a following ToggleOutputs() inverted a stale level. The copy now takes the riskier of the old and the asked value (configuration: output if either; output port: the written level; drive strength: the stronger code; 0x4F: push-pull if either; the other pairs: the written value), the register is marked unknown, and the next call that builds on it reads it first (one more read, only after a failure). A successful write of the pair, ReadOutputLatch() , ReadInputMask() , ReadPolarityInversion() , ApplyConfig() and EnsureInitialized() make it known again; the reset check never reads an unknown register. NoDevice (an address NACK) leaves the copy unchanged. An unknown register read back at its power-up value is DeviceReset (falsely, once, when the failed write's old or new value was the power-up value); with no other register to check, the reset check reads the unknown ones. A failed ApplyConfig() now leaves the new values of the registers written before the failure, the failed one unknown and the rest at their old values, instead of the previous configuration. SetDirection(..., Direction::Input) that leaves every pin an input writes only the configuration pair, with no reset check; releasing while other outputs remain writes the configuration pair before 0x4F and the output pair, so a failure after it leaves the pins released. The chip model can go through a power-on reset on its own in the middle of a session ( reset_after ), and the fuzzer chooses resets between calls.

docs.text: Configuration ¶ Every setting the driver writes, where it comes from, and how menuconfig sets it. Datasheet sections this page relies on Power-up value of every register: NXP PCAL9555A Rev. 2, Table 4 Command byte (power-up default), p. 6 Open-drain ports and the 0x4F write order: NXP PCAL9555A Rev. 2, 6.2.12 Output port configuration register (4Fh), p. 12 Registers, command bytes and power-up values: NXP PCA9555 Rev. 10, 6.2 Registers; 6.2.1 Command byte (Table 4), p. 6 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map . Config ¶ One pcal9555::Config holds every register the driver writes. Pass it to the constructor; EnsureInitialized() writes it and reads it back, and ApplyConfig() replaces it later. Its defaults are the power-up values of the registers (PCAL9555A data sheet table 4), so Config{} changes nothing on a freshly powered chip. constexpr pcal9555 :: Config BoardConfig () { pcal9555 :: Config c {}; // power-up values: every pin an input c . variant = pcal9555 :: Variant :: Pcal9555a ; // the part fitted has Agile I/O c . output_high_mask = 0x0000 ; // port 0 starts low... c . input_mask = 0xFF00 ; // ...and drives; port 1 stays inputs c . pull_enable_mask = 0xFF00 ; // pull resistors on port 1 only c . interrupt_mask = 0x00FF ; // port 1 raises INT, port 0 does not c . port0_mode = pcal9555 :: OutputMode :: OpenDrain ; return c ; } static_assert ( pcal9555 :: Validate ( BoardConfig ()) == pcal9555 :: Error :: Ok ); // checked at build time pcal9555 :: Error StartBoard ( MyPort & port ) { static pcal9555 :: PCAL9555 < MyPort > io ( port , 0x20 , BoardConfig ()); // stored, no I/O return io . EnsureInitialized (). error ; // written and read back } Bit n of each mask is pin n (P0_0 to P0_7 are pins 0 to 7, P1_0 to P1_7 pins 8 to 15). Field Register Power-up Meaning variant (driver side) Variant::Pca9555 Which part is fitted; Pcal9555a enables the fields below the line output_high_mask Output port 0x02, 0x03 0xFFFF 1 drives the pin high when it is an output polarity_invert_mask Polarity inversion 0x04, 0x05 0x0000 1 inverts how the input pin reads input_mask Configuration 0x06, 0x07 0xFFFF 1 = input, 0 = output drive_strength_codes Drive strength 0x40 to 0x43 0xFFFFFFFF Two bits per pin ( DriveStrength ), pin n at bits 2n+1..2n input_latch_mask Input latch 0x44, 0x45 0x0000 1 latches input changes until the port is read pull_enable_mask Pull enable 0x46, 0x47 0xFFFF 1 connects the pin's 100 kΩ resistor pull_up_mask Pull selection 0x48, 0x49 0xFFFF 1 = pull-up, 0 = pull-down interrupt_mask Interrupt mask 0x4A, 0x4B 0xFFFF 1 = the pin raises no interrupt port0_mode , port1_mode Output port configuration 0x4F PushPull OpenDrain for a whole port The fields from drive_strength_codes down exist on the PCAL9555A only. With variant = Variant::Pca9555 they must keep their power-up values: constexpr pcal9555 :: Config PlainPca9555 () { pcal9555 :: Config c {}; // variant = Pca9555: the registers both parts share c . input_mask = 0xFFF0 ; c . pull_up_mask = 0 ; // an Agile I/O field: Validate() and EnsureInitialized() say Unsupported return c ; } static_assert ( pcal9555 :: Validate ( PlainPca9555 ()) == pcal9555 :: Error :: Unsupported ); Write order ¶ EnsureInitialized() and ApplyConfig() write the Agile I/O bank first (drive strength, input latch, pull selection, pull enable, interrupt mask, then 0x4F), then the output port, the polarity inversion and last the configuration registers. The output stage and the output levels are therefore in place before any pin becomes an output, as the data sheet recommends for 0x4F (section 6.2.12), and no pin glitches to the power-up level. Validate ¶ pcal9555::Validate(config) checks a configuration without touching the chip, and is constexpr , so a configuration built at compile time can be checked with static_assert . It returns InvalidArgument when an enum holds a value that is not an enumerator, and Unsupported when variant is Pca9555 and an Agile I/O field differs from its power-up value. EnsureInitialized() and ApplyConfig() run it before any I/O. Every mask value is legal. Change it at run time ¶ pcal9555 :: Error Reconfigure ( pcal9555 :: PCAL9555 < MyPort >& io ) { pcal9555 :: Config c = io . GetConfig (); // the driver's copy, pin changes included c . interrupt_mask = 0x0000 ; // every pin raises INT from now on return io . ApplyConfig ( c ). error ; // running: written and read back; else stored } GetConfig() is the driver's copy of the registers: the configuration passed in, updated by every successful pin call. ApplyConfig() on a running driver writes every register and reads each back ( DeviceIdMismatch if one does not hold its value); before the start it only stores the configuration. The variant of a running driver cannot change ( InvalidArgument ): Deinitialize() first. The pin calls ( API guide ) change one register pair each and are cheaper for a few pins. Kconfig ¶ Under ESP-IDF, idf.py menuconfig shows PCA9555 / PCAL9555A GPIO expander when the driver is a component of the project ( Installation ); the menu is _config/Kconfig . The options reach the code only through inc/pcal9555_kconfig.hpp , never through a driver signature: pcal9555 :: Error StartFromMenuconfig ( MyPort & port ) { static pcal9555 :: PCAL9555 < MyPort > io ( port , 0x20 , pcal9555 :: KconfigDefaults ()); return io . EnsureInitialized (). error ; } Option Default Config field CONFIG_PCAL9555_VARIANT_PCA9555 , _PCAL9555A (a choice) PCA9555 variant CONFIG_PCAL9555_OUTPUT_HIGH_MASK (hex) 0xFFFF output_high_mask CONFIG_PCAL9555_INPUT_MASK (hex) 0xFFFF input_mask The I2C address is a constructor argument, not a Config field, so it is not a Kconfig option. Without Kconfig (plain CMake, other platforms) KconfigDefaults() returns Config{} . Both cases are host tests. Next: Porting .

docs.text: Contract ¶ What the PCAL9555 driver promises, what it needs, and the rules a caller follows. Datasheet sections this page relies on From NXP PCAL9555A Rev. 2: Power-up value of every register: Table 4 Command byte (power-up default), p. 6 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map . The driver inherits the Kokeb Labs driver contract ; this page states only what is specific to it. A change to anything here is a breaking change, listed under Breaking in the changelog . Promises ¶ The constructor is noexcept , stores the port, the address and the Config , does no I/O and cannot fail. EnsureInitialized() is the only start-up call. Its first call validates the stored Config and the address (no I/O when either is wrong), brings the bus up, checks that a part answers (and, for a PCAL9555A, that the reserved bits of 0x4F read 0), writes the identity pattern 0x55AA to the polarity inversion pair and reads it back, writes every register the driver owns and reads each back. On any failure the driver stays uninitialised and the next call starts again from the beginning. Once it has succeeded it returns Ok at once with no I/O. Every call that touches the chip returns Error::NotInitialized before EnsureInitialized() succeeds. No call starts, resets or reconfigures the chip as a side effect. ApplyConfig() before the start only stores the configuration; while running it writes every register and reads each back. A pin call makes only the transfers the data sheet needs; any read-back is opt-in, per call. Two checks are not opt-in, because the chip loses state on its own: SetDirection() , ApplyConfig() , CheckForReset() and a setter about to rewrite the register the reset check reads first read that register ( DeviceReset when it holds its power-up value, section 6.4), and SetDirection() writes 0x4F (PCAL9555A) and the output pair before the configuration pair (section 6.2.12). On a PCAL9555A with an unmasked input, ReadInputs() and ReadPin() read the interrupt status pair before the inputs clear it (sections 6.2.11, 6.5). With Verify::ReadBack as its last argument ( Verify::None by default), a setter reads its write back, and a register that did not keep its value returns Error::WriteMismatch : the call then never reports success for a write the chip acknowledged but lost. GetConfig() then holds what was asked for, so repeating an absolute call resends it (after ToggleOutputs() , resend with WriteOutputs(GetConfig().output_high_mask) ); ReadOutputLatch() , ReadInputMask() and ReadPolarityInversion() read what the chip holds. EnsureInitialized() and ApplyConfig() always read every register back. Every port failure propagates, as Error::NoDevice when the port's optional GetLastFailure() reports an address NACK and as Error::Bus otherwise; no call returns a stale or zero value after a failed read. After WriteMismatch the copy holds what was asked for, for each register pair that was sent. After a write that failed with Bus (its bytes may have arrived) the copy holds the riskier of the old and the asked value (an output rather than an input, the written level, the stronger drive, push-pull; the written value elsewhere) and the register is unknown: no call builds on it before reading it from the chip, and the reset check never reads it. After NoDevice (an address NACK: nothing arrived) the copy is unchanged. After a failed ApplyConfig() the registers written before the failure hold the new values, the one that failed is unknown, and the rest keep the old ones. ReadRegister() is one read with no retry. A port that does not satisfy I2cPort (exact hook types, noexcept , bool ), or an optional hook declared with another signature, is a compile error. At power-up every I/O is an input with a weak (about 100 kΩ) pull-up to VDD, so unused pins do not float. On the PCA9555 the pull-up is fixed (PCA9555 section 6.4); on the PCAL9555A it can be switched to a pull-down or off per pin ( Agile I/O ). Neither part has a reset pin: the only reset is the power-on reset, so the port has no GPIO hook. The pinout, the block diagram, the circuit and both tables are drawn from docs/hardware.yml . Inside the chip ¶ Figure 1 of the data sheet: SCL and SDA pass an input filter to the I2C-bus control, which moves 8 bits at a time to each port; an input change on either port drives INT through a low-pass filter. Inside the PCAL9555A Figure description and sources The PCAL9555A's function blocks inside its outline. Arrows between blocks carry signals or data in the direction they point (both ways where they have two heads). The package pins stand on the left and right edges with their numbers, each wired to the block it reaches. Drawn from: docs/hardware.yml ; inc/pcal9555_i2c_interface.hpp . The MCU and the expander share the 3.3 V supply, which sets the I2C logic levels ( Power ). PCAL9555A: Typical application Figure description and sources A schematic. Supply pins point up to their supply and decoupling, ground pins down. Pins on the right carry the loads and the pins tied to a supply or ground; a cross marks a pin left open. A dot is a junction; wires that cross without a dot are not connected. Drawn from: docs/hardware.yml ; inc/pcal9555_i2c_interface.hpp . Address ¶ 7-bit address 0100 A2 A1 A0 (section 6.1): 0x20 to 0x27 , eight chips per bus. AddressFromPins(a2, a1, a0) computes it; kI2cAddress (and its older name kDefaultI2cAddress ) is 0x20 . EnsureInitialized() rejects any other address with InvalidArgument before it touches the bus. Registers ¶ Table 4. The PCA9555 has the first eight registers; the PCAL9555A adds the Agile I/O bank. Pin n of the driver is bit n of a 16-bit pair: port 0 in the even register (bits 7..0), port 1 in the odd one. The register map Figure description and sources One card per register pair, in command-byte order; port 0 is the even byte, port 1 the odd one. The top band is the standard bank, 0x00 to 0x07, on both the PCA9555 and the PCAL9555A; the lower band is the Agile I/O bank, 0x40 to 0x4F, which only the PCAL9555A has. Each card gives the access (R or R/W), the power-up value of each register, the Config field the driver keeps for it, and the calls that read or write it. EnsureInitialized() and ApplyConfig() write every Config field shown. The input ports and the interrupt status are read only, so they have no Config field. After the address byte the master sends a command byte, which sets the pointer. Each data byte then goes to (or comes from) the pointed register, and the pointer moves to the other register of the pair : a write of two bytes after command 0x02 sets output port 0, then output port 1. Verify::None by default), add one read pair (113 µs) after each write pair and one read (90 µs) after the write of SetOutputMode() ( SetDirection() : one read pair after the configuration pair). The times are derived (9 clocks per byte), not measured, and leave out START, STOP and your port's overhead. Unimplemented command bytes ¶ Neither data sheet says how a part answers a command byte it does not implement, such as 0x4F on a PCA9555. The driver assumes a NACK and therefore never auto-detects the part: Config::variant names it. Configured as a PCAL9555A on a PCA9555 that NACKs, EnsureInitialized() fails with Bus at the 0x4F read, before any write. If a part instead used only the low three bits of the command, 0x4F would read configuration port 1, which is 0xFF after power-up; the reserved-bits check then fails with DeviceIdMismatch , still before any write. Not verified on hardware : bench step 4 in Troubleshooting checks it. Timing ¶ Neither part needs a wait between transfers: there is no conversion, no reset sequence and no programming time, so the driver never waits and the port has no DelayUs() hook. An input that changes raises INT; reading the input port of that pin releases it, as does the pin returning to its old level before the read. A pin configured as an output never raises INT, and turning an output into an input can raise a false interrupt when its level differs from the input register. PCA9555 PCAL9555A Which pins raise INT Every input, always Inputs whose interrupt mask bit is 0; all masked at power-up Which pin raised it Compare ReadInputs() with the last value ReadInterruptStatus() (masked pins read 0); the status does not clear INT Short pulses Lost if the pin returns before the read Kept with the input latch: the input register holds the level that raised INT until it is read Reading one port ( ReadPin() ) releases only that port's interrupt; ReadInputs() reads both. The read also clears the interrupt status bits of the port (section 6.2.11), so on a PCAL9555A with an unmasked input the driver reads the status pair into GetLatchedInterrupts() first. INT is open-drain, active low: pull it up to the MCU's VDD and wire it to an MCU input. The driver never runs in the ISR: signal a task, which then calls the driver ( API guide ). Power ¶ Parameter PCAL9555A PCA9555 Supply 1.65 V to 5.5 V 2.3 V to 5.5 V I/O 5.5 V tolerant 5.5 V tolerant Output sink current per pin 25 mA (drive strength 11b) 8 mA min at V_OL = 0.5 V Total ground current 200 mA (limiting value) 200 mA (limiting value) Total supply current (sourced by the I/Os) 160 mA (limiting value) 160 mA The supply sets the I2C logic levels: run the expander from the MCU's I/O voltage, or level-shift SDA and SCL. Power-on reset: every register returns to its power-up value when VDD rises from below the power-on reset voltage (section 6.4 and 8.3, which also give the required ramp and the glitch limits). After a brown-out the registers are back at their defaults while the driver still holds its copy: outputs high, push-pull, every pin an input. CheckForReset() , SetDirection() and ApplyConfig() find that and return DeviceReset , and SetDirection() writes 0x4F and the output pair before the directions, so a reset never turns the old outputs back on high: see API guide . Leakage: a pull-up or pull-down that fights an external level draws current; disconnect unused resistors with SetPull(mask, Pull::None) .
