docs.text: Neither data sheet says how a part answers a command byte it does not implement, such as 0x4F on a PCA9555. The driver assumes a NACK and therefore never auto-detects the part: Config::variant names it. Configured as a PCAL9555A on a PCA9555 that NACKs, EnsureInitialized() fails with Bus at the 0x4F read, before any write. If a part instead used only the low three bits of the command, 0x4F would read configuration port 1, which is 0xFF after power-up; the reserved-bits check then fails with DeviceIdMismatch , still before any write. Not verified on hardware : bench step 4 in Troubleshooting checks it.

docs.text: Section 6.5. An input that changes raises INT; reading the input port of that pin releases it, as does the pin returning to its old level before the read. A pin configured as an output never raises INT, and turning an output into an input can raise a false interrupt when its level differs from the input register. PCA9555 PCAL9555A Which pins raise INT Every input, always Inputs whose interrupt mask bit is 0; all masked at power-up Which pin raised it Compare ReadInputs() with the last value ReadInterruptStatus() (masked pins read 0); the status does not clear INT Short pulses Lost if the pin returns before the read Kept with the input latch: the input register holds the level that raised INT until it is read Reading one port ( ReadPin() ) releases only that port's interrupt; ReadInputs() reads both. The read also clears the interrupt status bits of the port (section 6.2.11), so on a PCAL9555A with an unmasked input the driver reads the status pair into GetLatchedInterrupts() first. INT is open-drain, active low: pull it up to the MCU's VDD and wire it to an MCU input. The driver never runs in the ISR: signal a task, which then calls the driver ( API guide ).

docs.text: Parameter PCAL9555A PCA9555 Supply 1.65 V to 5.5 V 2.3 V to 5.5 V I/O 5.5 V tolerant 5.5 V tolerant Output sink current per pin 25 mA (drive strength 11b) 8 mA min at V_OL = 0.5 V Total ground current 200 mA (limiting value) 200 mA (limiting value) Total supply current (sourced by the I/Os) 160 mA (limiting value) 160 mA The supply sets the I2C logic levels: run the expander from the MCU's I/O voltage, or level-shift SDA and SCL. Power-on reset: every register returns to its power-up value when VDD rises from below the power-on reset voltage (section 6.4 and 8.3, which also give the required ramp and the glitch limits). After a brown-out the registers are back at their defaults while the driver still holds its copy: outputs high, push-pull, every pin an input. CheckForReset() , SetDirection() and ApplyConfig() find that and return DeviceReset , and SetDirection() writes 0x4F and the output pair before the directions, so a reset never turns the old outputs back on high: see API guide . Leakage: a pull-up or pull-down that fights an external level draws current; disconnect unused resistors with SetPull(mask, Pull::None) .

docs.text: Installation ¶ Add the driver to a CMake project on any MCU or on your PC, or to an ESP-IDF project. It is a header-only C++20 library with no dependencies, and one root CMakeLists.txt serves every build. Requirements ¶ A C++20 compiler: GCC 10+, Clang 13+ or a current MSVC. The driver uses concepts and requires . CMake 3.16 or later: it generates the version header the driver includes ( pcal9555_version.h ). No RTOS, heap, exceptions or RTTI: every call is noexcept and returns a Result . Get the source ¶ A git submodule keeps the driver pinned to the version you chose: git submodule add https://github.com/kokeb-labs-drivers/driver-pcal9555.git external/driver-pcal9555 git submodule update --init external/driver-pcal9555 Only inc/ , src/ , cmake/ , _config/ and CMakeLists.txt are needed to build. The examples are not; the ESP32 example even has its own submodule ( examples/esp32/scripts ). CMake (any MCU, any host) ¶ This is the MCU-neutral path: the same two lines work for a host build, STM32 (CubeMX CMake projects), RP2040 (Pico SDK), nRF (nRF Connect SDK) or any other CMake toolchain. Platforms lists what has a port today. add_subdirectory ( external/driver-pcal9555 ) target_link_libraries ( my_app PRIVATE pcal9555::pcal9555 ) pcal9555::pcal9555 is an alias of the pcal9555 INTERFACE target. It carries the include directories (the headers and the generated version header) and requires C++20, so your target does not need to set either. Option Default Effect PCAL9555_ENABLE_WARNINGS OFF -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic on every target that links the driver PCAL9555_BUILD_TESTS OFF Builds the host tests in tests/ and the host example ( Testing and CI ) Installed package ¶ To use the driver without adding its source tree to your build, install it and find the package: cmake -S external/driver-pcal9555 -B build-pcal9555 cmake --install build-pcal9555 --prefix /opt/sdk find_package ( pcal9555 0.1 REQUIRED ) # with CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=/opt/sdk target_link_libraries ( my_app PRIVATE pcal9555::pcal9555 ) The target is pcal9555::pcal9555 in both cases ( EXPORT_NAME ), so a project can switch between add_subdirectory() and find_package() without changing its target_link_libraries() . The headers and the generated pcal9555_version.h go to include/pcal9555/inc/ , the template implementation to include/pcal9555/src/pcal9555.ipp . The host CI installs the package and builds a consumer against it on every pull request ( Testing and CI ). ESP-IDF ¶ Under ESP-IDF the root CMakeLists.txt registers the repository itself as a component: with ESP_PLATFORM set it calls idf_component_register() from the same build settings, with the menu in _config/Kconfig . There is no wrapper to copy. ESP-IDF names a component after its folder, so the name in your REQUIRES is the name of the folder the repository is in. Pick one of these: How What to write Component name Folder of extra components list(APPEND EXTRA_COMPONENT_DIRS external/driver-pcal9555) in the project CMakeLists.txt , before project.cmake driver-pcal9555 (the folder) Submodule under components/ git submodule add https://github.com/kokeb-labs-drivers/driver-pcal9555.git components/pcal9555 pcal9555 (the folder) Component manager, from git The dependency below in main/idf_component.yml pcal9555 (the key) # main/idf_component.yml of your project dependencies : pcal9555 : git : https://github.com/kokeb-labs-drivers/driver-pcal9555.git version : v0.1.0 # a release tag Your component then declares REQUIRES pcal9555 (or the folder name), and idf.py menuconfig shows the driver's menu ( Configuration ). The ESP32 example uses the first way, with EXTRA_COMPONENT_DIRS pointing at the repository root, and works out the folder name in main/CMakeLists.txt ; CI builds it on every pull request. The repository has no idf_component.yml . The component manager does not need one for a git dependency; the manifest is only required to publish to the ESP Component Registry, which these releases do not use. If registry publishing is chosen, the manifest is added at the root then. How the build is organised ¶ Layer File Role Settings cmake/pcal9555_build_settings.cmake Target name, include directories, sources, version: the single source of truth Library CMakeLists.txt INTERFACE target, alias, install rules and the package export, or the ESP-IDF component Tool configuration _config/ Doxyfile, the docs site, Kconfig, clang-format, clang-tidy and the linters Version ¶ The version is set once in the settings file and written into pcal9555_version.h in the build tree at configure time. The Doxyfile ( _config/Doxyfile ) carries a copy; a host test fails when it differs. Read it at run time: const char * v = pcal9555 :: GetDriverVersion (); // "0.1.0" Next ¶ Quickstart runs the driver on your PC, then on your MCU; Porting writes the port for your MCU.

docs.text: Status and limitations ¶ What this driver has and has not been shown to do, so you can decide whether it is ready for your use. Status ¶ Version 0.1.0, not released On hardware This driver is not verified yet : see Before you depend on it Tested against A protocol model of both parts ( Testing and CI ), a fuzzer and the quality gates Assurance level high (Kokeb Labs handbook): not qualified for use in a safety function Design choices the data sheets call for ¶ Each of these follows from the PCAL9555A data sheet (Rev. 2); the Datasheet map links the sections. An acknowledged write can still be lost or altered. An I2C acknowledge confirms that a byte was received; it carries no checksum, and the data sheet itself allows for a "glitch or data corruption" (section 8.3). The output port registers read back the value written, not the pin (section 6.2.3), so a read-back shows what the chip holds. The driver reads a write back when the call asks for it ( Verify::ReadBack , the last argument of every setter; off by default) and then returns WriteMismatch ; the model can drop writes, and the tests and the fuzzer cover it. Reading the inputs does not identify the part. The input ports hold the pin levels (section 6.2.2), so any value is plausible, and a device that acknowledges every byte answers the read. At start-up the driver writes a test pattern to the polarity inversion pair, which changes only how inputs read (section 6.2.4), and reads it back, then writes every register and reads each back. Outputs are written before directions , so no pin glitches: a pin that becomes an output drives its output latch at once (section 6.2.5), and the latch is high after power-up (table 4). A power-on reset is found in the registers. Neither part has a reset pin or a reset flag; a supply dip below the power-on reset voltage reloads every register (section 6.4, table 4): outputs high, push-pull, every pin an input. The driver reads one register whose copy differs from its power-up value ( CheckForReset() , and first in SetDirection() , ApplyConfig() and a setter about to rewrite that register) and returns DeviceReset , uninitialised, instead of writing its copy over a reset chip. A SetDirection() that makes pins outputs writes 0x4F, the output pair and the configuration pair, in that order (section 6.2.12), so even a reset between its check and its writes never turns a pin into an output at the reset level. Releasing pins is the safe direction and goes the other way: when every pin ends up an input the configuration pair is the only transfer, with no check; when outputs remain, the check, then the configuration pair first, then 0x4F and the output pair for the pins that stay outputs. A reset in the microseconds between that check and the configuration write leaves those remaining outputs at the power-up level until the two writes after it land. A dropped write to the checked register reads as a reset, with the same recovery. A reset is found at the next check, not when it happens: call CheckForReset() as often as a dip matters. A failed write may have arrived. An I2C failure can come after the bytes were clocked in (a NACK of the last byte, a lost ACK). After a write that failed with Bus the copy takes the riskier of the old and the asked value (an output rather than an input, the written level, the stronger drive, push-pull) and the register is unknown until a read or a successful write; the next call that builds on it reads it first. An unknown register read back at its power-up value is taken as a reset ( DeviceReset ), and any other value is adopted; the reset check never reads an unknown register as its sentinel, and with no other register to read it reads the unknown ones. The rule needs no record of what the failed write may have left, at a price: when that write's old or new value was the power-up value, the read gives one false DeviceReset . Nothing is written, EnsureInitialized() writes the copy again, and nothing stays stuck. GetConfig() shows the riskier value for the direction, the drive strength and 0x4F, but the written level for the outputs, which is not necessarily what the pins do: ReadOutputLatch() reads it. An input read latches the interrupt status first. Reading an input port clears its interrupt status (sections 6.2.11, 6.5), so with an unmasked input on a PCAL9555A the driver reads the status pair before the inputs, into GetLatchedInterrupts() : one more read per input read. The two reads are separate transfers: an edge between them sets a status bit that the input read then clears (section 6.5), so that bit never reaches GetLatchedInterrupts() . The edge still shows in the level the input read returns (with the input latch, the latched level), so compare the returned value with the last one ( GetLastInputs() ) when no edge may be missed. The driver never waits. The chip has no busy state and needs no delay between transfers (section 7), so a call's duration is the port's transfers; the port's timeout bounds every call ( API guide ). What the model cannot show ¶ The model is written from the data sheets by the same reading as the driver. It cannot show: how a PCA9555 answers the PCAL9555A-only command 0x4F. The driver assumes a NACK (or a value with reserved bits set), so that a PCAL9555A configuration on a PCA9555 fails at start-up; no PCA9555 has been tried; electrical behaviour: drive strength, the 100 kΩ pulls, open-drain levels, the INT pin's timing; what another master does to the registers between two calls. A supply dip is modelled as the data sheet describes it, every register back at its power-up value (section 6.4); how a real supply ramp behaves near the power-on reset voltage, and whether a partial dip can leave some registers changed, is not verified on hardware (bench step 7 in Troubleshooting ). docs.text: Porting ¶ Run the driver on a new MCU by writing one class: the port. Datasheet sections this page relies on From NXP PCAL9555A Rev. 2: Address pins and the 7-bit address: 6.1 Device address, p. 5 Register pairs, pointer toggling and burst transfers: 7 Bus transactions; 7.1 Writing to the port registers; 7.2 Reading the port registers, p. 14 I2C timing and INT timing: 13 Dynamic characteristics, p. 32 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map . The driver never calls your SDK. It calls hooks on a class you derive from pcal9555::I2cInterface<Self> (in inc/pcal9555_i2c_interface.hpp ). The base uses CRTP and declares no hook itself; the driver template is constrained by the pcal9555::I2cPort concept, so calls are resolved at compile time (no virtual functions, nothing to allocate) and a missing or misdeclared hook is a compile error at the point of use. What you implement ¶ Method Required Contract bool EnsureInitialized() noexcept yes Bring the bus up on the first call; return true at once afterwards. false makes the driver's EnsureInitialized() return Bus bool Write(uint8_t addr, const uint8_t* data, std::size_t len) noexcept yes START, addr + W, len bytes, STOP. false on a NACK or any bus error bool WriteRead(uint8_t addr, const uint8_t* tx, std::size_t tx_len, uint8_t* rx, std::size_t rx_len) noexcept yes START, addr + W, tx , repeated START, addr + R, rx_len bytes (NACK the last), STOP void Log(LogLevel, const char* message) noexcept no Print one line; message is plain text, never a format string bool GetLastFailure(I2cFailure& failure) noexcept no After Write() or WriteRead() returned false : set failure and return true when the controller knows why, return false when it cannot tell addr is the 7-bit address the driver was constructed with; shift it yourself if your SDK wants the 8-bit form. The chip needs no delay and has no reset pin, so there is no DelayUs() and no GpioSet() hook. Bus requirements ¶ What the chip needs from the bus is in inc/pcal9555_i2c_interface.hpp as constexpr values (handbook KB-CPP-123). Check your port's settings against them with static_assert , so that a port that clocks too fast does not compile: Constant Value Meaning Data sheet kI2cAddress 0x20 The base 7-bit address, A2, A1 and A0 low; the pins add 0 to 7 ( AddressFromPins() , 0x20 to 0x27) PCAL9555A 6.1, figure 4 kMaxClockHz 400'000 The highest SCL frequency: standard or fast mode PCAL9555A 13, table 33 (f_SCL) kRepeatedStart true A register read is a write of the command byte, a repeated START, then the read PCAL9555A 7.2 inline constexpr uint32_t kMyClockHz = 400'000 ; static_assert ( kMyClockHz <= pcal9555 :: kMaxClockHz , "SCL above the PCAL9555's maximum" ); static_assert ( pcal9555 :: kRepeatedStart , "WriteRead() must use a repeated START" ); Both example ports do this, and the ESP32 port also checks that its address is 0x20 to 0x27. NACKs. The chip NACKs no transfer the driver sends by design: it has no reset command and no busy state, and the driver sends only the command bytes the configured part implements (0x00 to 0x07, and on the PCAL9555A 0x40 to 0x4D and 0x4F). The NACK the master sends on the last byte it reads ends the read; it is not a failure. A NACK the port reports is therefore always a fault: no chip at the address ( NoDevice with GetLastFailure() , Bus without it), or a part that refuses a command byte, such as a PCA9555 configured as a PCAL9555A, if it NACKs the Agile I/O command byte ( Bus ; see Hardware ). The driver never probes with an empty or zero-length transfer: every transfer carries the command byte (handbook KB-CPP-130). Pins. The chip has no control input the port drives: no reset, no enable, no chip select. A2 to A0 are strapped on the board. INT is an open-drain output of the chip, active low, idle high through the board's pull-up; read it on an MCU input. The expander's own pins power up as inputs (configuration registers 0xFFFF), and EnsureInitialized() writes the output levels before the directions, so a pin that becomes an output starts at its configured level (handbook KB-HW-018). The port ¶ my_port.hpp class MyPort : public pcal9555 :: I2cInterface < MyPort > { public : // Bring the bus up once; later calls return true at once. bool EnsureInitialized () noexcept { if ( ! ready_ ) { ready_ = platform_i2c_init (); } return ready_ ; } // One write transaction: START, address + W, the bytes (command byte first), STOP. bool Write ( uint8_t addr , const uint8_t * data , std :: size_t len ) noexcept { return platform_i2c_write ( addr , data , len ); } // Write then read with a repeated START in between. bool WriteRead ( uint8_t addr , const uint8_t * tx , std :: size_t tx_len , uint8_t * rx , std :: size_t rx_len ) noexcept { return platform_i2c_write_read ( addr , tx , tx_len , rx , rx_len ); } private : bool ready_ = false ; }; Rules the transfers must follow: One call, one transaction. The command byte is the first byte of Write() and the tx of WriteRead() ; never split a pair: the chip toggles between the two registers of a pair only within one transaction. Repeated START for WriteRead() , no STOP between the write and the read. Raw bytes only. Do not retry; the driver owns the framing. Return false for a NACK or a bus error. The driver turns it into Error::Bus , or Error::NoDevice when GetLastFailure() says nothing acknowledged the address. Bounded time-outs. A stuck bus fails the call; it does not block forever. Up to 400 kHz ( kMaxClockHz ). Both parts support standard and fast mode. Optional hooks ¶ The driver finds the optional hooks at compile time with C++20 requires , in one place ( pcal9555::detail , in inc/pcal9555_i2c_interface.hpp ). A hook that is declared with the wrong signature, for example without noexcept or returning void , is a compile error that names it; it is never silently ignored. Hook Used for Without it Log() One line per lifecycle event or failure Nothing is logged GetLastFailure() Telling an address NACK from other failures, so that an absent or unpowered chip is NoDevice Every failed transfer is Bus GetLastFailure() reports on the last failed transfer only, with I2cFailure::AddressNack (nothing acknowledged the address), DataNack (the address was acknowledged, a data byte was not) or Other (a stuck line, lost arbitration, a timeout). Only AddressNack changes what the driver returns. Return false when the controller cannot tell: ESP-IDF's i2c_master , for one, reports a NACK without saying which byte it was, so the ESP32 example port has no GetLastFailure() and an absent chip is Bus with it. A port with both hooks: class FullPort : public pcal9555 :: I2cInterface < FullPort > { public : bool EnsureInitialized () noexcept { return platform_i2c_init (); } bool Write ( uint8_t addr , const uint8_t * data , std :: size_t len ) noexcept { return platform_i2c_write ( addr , data , len ); } bool WriteRead ( uint8_t addr , const uint8_t * tx , std :: size_t tx_len , uint8_t * rx , std :: size_t rx_len ) noexcept { return platform_i2c_write_read ( addr , tx , tx_len , rx , rx_len ); } // Optional: one line per lifecycle event or failure. The driver never formats; the port does. void Log ( pcal9555 :: LogLevel level , const char * message ) noexcept { if ( level > pcal9555 :: LogLevel :: Warning ) { return ; } platform_log ( message ); // plain text: never use it as a format string } // Optional: why the last Write() or WriteRead() failed. With it an absent chip is // Error::NoDevice; without it, or when this returns false, every failure is Error::Bus. bool GetLastFailure ( pcal9555 :: I2cFailure & failure ) noexcept { switch ( platform_i2c_last_nack ()) { case 1 : failure = pcal9555 :: I2cFailure :: AddressNack ; return true ; case 2 : failure = pcal9555 :: I2cFailure :: DataNack ; return true ; default : return false ; // the controller cannot tell } } }; Several chips on one bus ¶ One port can serve up to eight expanders: each driver object has its own address and its own copy of the registers. // Two expanders on one bus share the port; each driver object has its own address. bool BringUpBoth ( FullPort & bus ) { pcal9555 :: PCAL9555 < FullPort > left ( bus , pcal9555 :: AddressFromPins ( false , false , false )); // 0x20 pcal9555 :: PCAL9555 < FullPort > right ( bus , pcal9555 :: AddressFromPins ( false , false , true )); // 0x21 return left . EnsureInitialized (). ok () && right . EnsureInitialized (). ok (); } The port must then serialise the bus if the drivers run in different tasks ( Contract ). Reference implementations ¶ Every port lives with its example, in examples/<platform>/ ; the driver has none. Platforms lists them and how to add one. examples/host/host_pcal9555_port.hpp : any PC, against a simulated chip, with Log() and GetLastFailure() . Start from it for a host build or a test bench; it is also the smallest complete port. examples/esp32/main/esp32_pcal9555_port.hpp : ESP-IDF, with the log hook. Start from it for any ESP-IDF target. Check your port ¶ Build it: the ports on this page are compiled by the host CI from tests/docs/ , with the driver instantiated over them. Call EnsureInitialized() : Ok proves that writes and repeated-START reads work, since every register is read back. Toggle an output with ToggleOutputs() and watch it, then read an input with ReadPin() . Threads ¶ The driver is not thread-safe. Give each driver object one owner task, or guard every call with one mutex. When several chips share a bus, the port must also serialise the bus. See Contract . Editor setup ¶ The clang-format and clang-tidy configuration is in _config/ , and the repository root has no copy of it. Tools that take a path use it directly; CI does the same: Tool Setting Command line clang-format --style=file:_config/.clang-format , clang-tidy --config-file=_config/.clang-tidy -p build VS Code (C/C++ extension) "C_Cpp.clang_format_style": "file:${workspaceFolder}/_config/.clang-format" and "C_Cpp.codeAnalysis.clangTidy.args": ["--config-file=${workspaceFolder}/_config/.clang-tidy"] clangd (VS Code clangd, Neovim, Emacs), CLion These find .clang-format and .clang-tidy only by name, from the file upwards: copy both to the root once ( cp _config/.clang-format _config/.clang-tidy . ). .gitignore lists the copies, so they never reach a commit; copy again after _config/ changes Configure with -DCMAKE_EXPORT_COMPILE_COMMANDS=ON (clangd: --compile-commands-dir=build ) so the editor sees the same flags as the build.

docs.text: my_port.hpp class MyPort : public pcal9555 :: I2cInterface < MyPort > { public : // Bring the bus up once; later calls return true at once. bool EnsureInitialized () noexcept { if ( ! ready_ ) { ready_ = platform_i2c_init (); } return ready_ ; } // One write transaction: START, address + W, the bytes (command byte first), STOP. bool Write ( uint8_t addr , const uint8_t * data , std :: size_t len ) noexcept { return platform_i2c_write ( addr , data , len ); } // Write then read with a repeated START in between. bool WriteRead ( uint8_t addr , const uint8_t * tx , std :: size_t tx_len , uint8_t * rx , std :: size_t rx_len ) noexcept { return platform_i2c_write_read ( addr , tx , tx_len , rx , rx_len ); } private : bool ready_ = false ; }; Rules the transfers must follow: One call, one transaction. The command byte is the first byte of Write() and the tx of WriteRead() ; never split a pair: the chip toggles between the two registers of a pair only within one transaction. Repeated START for WriteRead() , no STOP between the write and the read. Raw bytes only. Do not retry; the driver owns the framing. Return false for a NACK or a bus error. The driver turns it into Error::Bus , or Error::NoDevice when GetLastFailure() says nothing acknowledged the address. Bounded time-outs. A stuck bus fails the call; it does not block forever. Up to 400 kHz ( kMaxClockHz ). Both parts support standard and fast mode.
docs.title: The port

docs.text: The driver finds the optional hooks at compile time with C++20 requires , in one place ( pcal9555::detail , in inc/pcal9555_i2c_interface.hpp ). A hook that is declared with the wrong signature, for example without noexcept or returning void , is a compile error that names it; it is never silently ignored. Hook Used for Without it Log() One line per lifecycle event or failure Nothing is logged GetLastFailure() Telling an address NACK from other failures, so that an absent or unpowered chip is NoDevice Every failed transfer is Bus GetLastFailure() reports on the last failed transfer only, with I2cFailure::AddressNack (nothing acknowledged the address), DataNack (the address was acknowledged, a data byte was not) or Other (a stuck line, lost arbitration, a timeout). Only AddressNack changes what the driver returns. Return false when the controller cannot tell: ESP-IDF's i2c_master , for one, reports a NACK without saying which byte it was, so the ESP32 example port has no GetLastFailure() and an absent chip is Bus with it. A port with both hooks: class FullPort : public pcal9555 :: I2cInterface < FullPort > { public : bool EnsureInitialized () noexcept { return platform_i2c_init (); } bool Write ( uint8_t addr , const uint8_t * data , std :: size_t len ) noexcept { return platform_i2c_write ( addr , data , len ); } bool WriteRead ( uint8_t addr , const uint8_t * tx , std :: size_t tx_len , uint8_t * rx , std :: size_t rx_len ) noexcept { return platform_i2c_write_read ( addr , tx , tx_len , rx , rx_len ); } // Optional: one line per lifecycle event or failure. The driver never formats; the port does. void Log ( pcal9555 :: LogLevel level , const char * message ) noexcept { if ( level > pcal9555 :: LogLevel :: Warning ) { return ; } platform_log ( message ); // plain text: never use it as a format string } // Optional: why the last Write() or WriteRead() failed. With it an absent chip is // Error::NoDevice; without it, or when this returns false, every failure is Error::Bus. bool GetLastFailure ( pcal9555 :: I2cFailure & failure ) noexcept { switch ( platform_i2c_last_nack ()) { case 1 : failure = pcal9555 :: I2cFailure :: AddressNack ; return true ; case 2 : failure = pcal9555 :: I2cFailure :: DataNack ; return true ; default : return false ; // the controller cannot tell } } };

Try it on your PC ¶ examples/host/ runs the real driver against a simulated PCAL9555A, through a host port. Wire it ¶ MCU PCA9555 / PCAL9555A Notes I2C SCL SCL Pull-up to VDD; 4.7 kΩ suits 100 kHz and 400 kHz I2C SDA SDA Pull-up to VDD GND A0, A1, A2 Address 0x20 ( kI2cAddress ); never leave them open 3.3 V VDD 100 nF to GND close to the pin GND VSS P0_0 LED and resistor to GND, for this example P1_0 Push button to GND, and a pull-up (the PCAL9555A has one built in) INT is optional: leave it open for this example, or pull it up and wire it to an MCU input. The Hardware page has the full pin list. 2. Add the driver ¶ Add the repository as a submodule and link the pcal9555::pcal9555 CMake target. Installation covers CMake on any MCU, the installed package and ESP-IDF. git submodule add https://github.com/kokeb-labs-drivers/driver-pcal9555.git external/driver-pcal9555 3. Write the port ¶ The port is the only platform code: it brings the bus up and moves bytes. Replace the platform_* calls with your SDK's. my_port.hpp class MyPort : public pcal9555 :: I2cInterface < MyPort > { public : // Bring the bus up once; later calls return true at once. bool EnsureInitialized () noexcept { if ( ! ready_ ) { ready_ = platform_i2c_init (); } return ready_ ; } // One write transaction: START, address + W, the bytes (command byte first), STOP. bool Write ( uint8_t addr , const uint8_t * data , std :: size_t len ) noexcept { return platform_i2c_write ( addr , data , len ); } // Write then read with a repeated START in between. bool WriteRead ( uint8_t addr , const uint8_t * tx , std :: size_t tx_len , uint8_t * rx , std :: size_t rx_len ) noexcept { return platform_i2c_write_read ( addr , tx , tx_len , rx , rx_len ); } private : bool ready_ = false ; }; Porting explains each method, the optional hook and the transfer rules. 4. Blink and read ¶ main.cpp #include "pcal9555.hpp" int blink_and_read ( MyPort & port , bool & button_pressed ) { pcal9555 :: PCAL9555 < MyPort > io ( port , 0x20 ); // A2..A0 low; no I/O yet if ( auto r = io . EnsureInitialized (); ! r ) { // 1. bus up, presence, Config{} written, checked return static_cast < int > ( r . error ); // Bus: nothing at 0x20; DeviceIdMismatch: another part } const uint16_t led = pcal9555 :: PinMask ( 0 ); // P0_0 drives an LED to ground if ( auto r = io . SetOutputs ( led , true ); ! r ) { // 2. level first, then direction: no glitch return static_cast < int > ( r . error ); } if ( auto r = io . SetDirection ( led , pcal9555 :: Direction :: Output ); ! r ) { return static_cast < int > ( r . error ); } const auto button = io . ReadPin ( 8 ); // 3. P1_0: a button to ground, pulled up externally if ( ! button ) { return static_cast < int > ( button . error ); } button_pressed = ! button . value ; return 0 ; } What each step does: EnsureInitialized() calls your port's EnsureInitialized() , reads the input ports to see that a chip ACKs 0x20, writes Config{} (the power-up values: every pin an input, every output latch high) and reads each register back. A second call returns Ok at once with no I/O. SetOutputs() sets the output latch of P0_0 high first, then SetDirection() makes it an output, so the pin never drives low in between. Each is one 3-byte write. ReadPin(8) reads input port 1 and returns P1_0; the button pulls it low when pressed. This example is built by the host CI, so it compiles against the current headers. If it does not work ¶ Symptom First thing to check EnsureInitialized() returns Bus Nothing ACKs the address: A2..A0 levels, SDA and SCL pull-ups, VDD ( Troubleshooting ) EnsureInitialized() returns DeviceIdMismatch Another part answers at that address, or Config::variant names a PCAL9555A on a PCA9555 EnsureInitialized() returns Unsupported An Agile I/O field is set in Config while variant is Pca9555 The LED does not light The pin is still an input: SetDirection(..., Direction::Output) Next ¶ API guide : outputs, inputs, interrupts, errors. docs.text: Testing and CI ¶ How the driver is checked: host tests against a model of the chip, a fuzzer that fails, loses and replaces bus transfers, compiled documentation, an install test, ESP32 and Cortex-M builds, static analysis and measured quality gates, on every pull request. Host tests ¶ The tests build the real driver against a protocol model of the PCA9555 and PCAL9555A: the command byte and the pointer that toggles within a register pair, power-up values, 16 pins with outputs, open-drain stages and an external level a test sets, the interrupt with its mask, status and input latch, a power-on reset in the middle of a session that reloads every power-up value on its own (section 6.4, reset_after ), a write that arrives but is reported failed ( stored_then_fail ), and injected faults (a transfer that fails, no chip at the address, a part that NACKs or aliases the Agile I/O command bytes, a register that drops writes, writes acknowledged and lost, reserved bits that read 1, a deaf device that acknowledges everything) and bus line modes (SDA floating high, so no address is acknowledged, or stuck low). They build as ISO C++20 with -pedantic-errors and the firmware's flags, -fno-exceptions -fno-rtti , and warnings as errors, on GCC and Clang. The model stands alone (handbook KB-TST-030): tests/mock_pcal9555.hpp includes no driver header and carries its own register map and power-up values, each with its data sheet section, so a constant the driver gets wrong cannot hide behind the same wrong constant in the model. tests/test_model.cpp checks the two maps against each other with static_assert : // Command bytes (section 6.2.1, table 4). static_assert ( chip :: kInputPort0 == reg :: kInputPort0 && chip :: kOutputPort0 == reg :: kOutputPort0 && chip :: kPolarityPort0 == reg :: kPolarityPort0 && chip :: kConfigPort0 == reg :: kConfigPort0 ); static_assert ( chip :: kDriveStrength0 == reg :: kDriveStrength0 && chip :: kDriveStrength2 == reg :: kDriveStrength2 && chip :: kInputLatch0 == reg :: kInputLatch0 && chip :: kPullEnable0 == reg :: kPullEnable0 && chip :: kPullSelect0 == reg :: kPullSelect0 && chip :: kInterruptMask0 == reg :: kInterruptMask0 && chip :: kInterruptStatus0 == reg :: kInterruptStatus0 && chip :: kOutputPortConfig == reg :: kOutputPortConfig ); // The output port configuration register (section 6.2.12, table 27). static_assert ( chip :: kOden0 == reg :: kOutputConfigOden0 && chip :: kOden1 == reg :: kOutputConfigOden1 && chip :: kOutputConfigReserved == reg :: kOutputConfigReservedMask ); // Power-up values (table 4). static_assert ( chip :: kOutputReset == reg :: kOutputReset && chip :: kPolarityReset == reg :: kPolarityReset && chip :: kConfigReset == reg :: kConfigReset && chip :: kInputLatchReset == reg :: kInputLatchReset && chip :: kPullEnableReset == reg :: kPullEnableReset && chip :: kPullSelectReset == reg :: kPullSelectReset && chip :: kInterruptMaskReset == reg :: kInterruptMaskReset && chip :: kOutputPortConfigReset == reg :: kOutputPortConfigReset ); static_assert (( static_cast < uint32_t > ( chip :: kDriveStrengthReset ) << 16U | chip :: kDriveStrengthReset ) == reg :: kDriveStrengthReset ); // The implemented command bytes: the model NACKs exactly the ones the driver never sends. static_assert ( chip :: kLastStandard == reg :: kConfigPort0 + 1U ); // The bus (section 6.1, section 13 table 33). static_assert ( chip :: kBaseAddress == pcal9555 :: kI2cAddress && chip :: kMaxClockHz == pcal9555 :: kMaxClockHz ); Two mock ports drive it: BarePort has only the required hooks, so every failed transfer is Bus ; FullPort adds Log() and GetLastFailure() , so an address NACK is NoDevice . Every public header is also compiled alone, as ISO C++20 with -pedantic-errors , by the target pcal9555_header_checks ; each generated unit asserts __cplusplus == 202002L (handbook KB-CPP20-001). The Cortex-M cross-build compiles the same units, and the ESP-IDF build compiles examples/esp32/main/pcal9555_cxx20_check.cpp at -std=c++20 -pedantic-errors , because ESP-IDF builds the rest of the application in a newer GNU dialect. cmake -S . -B build -DPCAL9555_BUILD_TESTS = ON cmake --build build ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure File Covers tests/test_pcal9555.cpp Lifecycle, presence and identity checks, configuration, pins, Agile I/O, the variant, the log hook tests/test_diagnostics.cpp NoDevice with and without GetLastFailure() , the floating, stuck and deaf bus on start-up and every read, ReadRegister() , GetLastInputs() , GetLastOutput() , the interrupt latch, the optional-hook concepts tests/test_model.cpp The model's register map against the driver's, at compile time; the model implements exactly the command bytes reg::IsImplemented() allows tests/test_bus_faults.cpp Every transfer of every operation, the start-up included, failed in turn and reported as Bus , through both mock port types tests/fuzz/ The fuzz target; CTest replays its corpus ( pcal9555_fuzz_pcal9555_corpus ), see below tests/test_errors.cpp The base Error values are 0 to 9; every chip-specific value (16 and up) is returned by some call tests/test_version.cpp The version getters follow the generated header (also against a 9.8.7 probe) tests/test_kconfig.cpp KconfigDefaults() with and without CONFIG_ values tests/compile_fail/ Code that must not compile, for its EXPECT: diagnostic: a class that is not a port, a hook with a narrower length or without noexcept , a misdeclared optional Log() or GetLastFailure() tests/mock_pcal9555.hpp The protocol model, independent of the driver's headers; docs.text: Troubleshooting ¶ Symptoms, causes and fixes, cheapest check first. Datasheet sections this page relies on Address pins and the 7-bit address: NXP PCAL9555A Rev. 2, 6.1 Device address, p. 5 Input latch: NXP PCAL9555A Rev. 2, 6.2.7 Input latch register pair, p. 9 Pull-up and pull-down resistors: NXP PCAL9555A Rev. 2, 6.2.8 Pull-up/pull-down enable register pair; 6.2.9 Pull-up/pull-down selection register pair, p. 10 Interrupt mask: NXP PCAL9555A Rev. 2, 6.2.10 Interrupt mask register pair, p. 11 Open-drain ports and the 0x4F write order: NXP PCAL9555A Rev. 2, 6.2.12 Output port configuration register (4Fh), p. 12 Power-on reset: NXP PCAL9555A Rev. 2, 6.4 Power-on reset; 8.3 Power-on reset requirements, p. 13 Interrupt output (INT): NXP PCAL9555A Rev. 2, 6.5 Interrupt output, p. 14 Power-on reset: NXP PCA9555 Rev. 10, 6.3 Power-on reset, p. 8 All of them, with the driver API for each: Datasheet map . EnsureInitialized returns NoDevice ¶ Nothing acknowledged the address: the port's GetLastFailure() saw the address byte NACKed. Check the supply of the expander, then A2, A1 and A0 against the address you passed ( AddressFromPins(a2, a1, a0) ). A port without GetLastFailure() reports the same fault as Bus . EnsureInitialized returns Bus ¶ The port reported a failure: its EnsureInitialized() returned false , or a transfer did. Without the optional GetLastFailure() hook the driver cannot tell a NACK from a bus error, so the first transfer failing usually means that nothing answers at the address; with it, Bus means the bus itself failed (a stuck line, lost arbitration, a timeout) or the part refused a command byte. Check that your port's EnsureInitialized() returns true on its own (log it). Check A2, A1 and A0 against the address you passed: AddressFromPins(a2, a1, a0) . The pins must be tied to VDD or VSS, never left open. Check the pull-ups on SDA and SCL (to the expander's VDD) and the supply. Read input port 0 at the address with your SDK (one write of 0x00, a repeated START, a one-byte read): an address that answers here and not in the driver points at the port's address handling (7-bit, not shifted). Avoid zero-length "scan" transfers; the driver never sends one (handbook KB-CPP-130). With Variant::Pcal9555a : a failure at the second transfer (the 0x4F read) means the part NACKs the Agile I/O bank, so it is a PCA9555. Use Variant::Pca9555 . EnsureInitialized returns DeviceIdMismatch ¶ Something answers at the address, but a register did not read back what was written, or a reserved bit of 0x4F read 1 on a driver configured for the PCAL9555A. Symptom Likely cause Fix Only with Variant::Pcal9555a A PCA9555 that does not NACK 0x4F Use Variant::Pca9555 , or fit a PCAL9555A With either variant Another part at the address (a different I/O expander, an EEPROM page, a sensor) Check the part number and the address pins Now and then Corrupted bytes on the bus Lower the clock; check the pull-ups and the wiring length EnsureInitialized returns Unsupported ¶ An Agile I/O field of Config differs from its power-up value while variant is Pca9555 . Set variant = Variant::Pcal9555a if a PCAL9555A is fitted, or leave the field at its default. EnsureInitialized returns InvalidArgument ¶ The address is outside 0x20 to 0x27 (an 8-bit address such as 0x40 is the 7-bit 0x20 shifted), or a Config field holds a value that is not an enumerator. Nothing was sent. A call returns DeviceReset ¶ The driver found a register back at its power-up value while its copy says otherwise: the expander went through a power-on reset (a supply dip below the power-on reset voltage, section 6.4), or the chip dropped a write to that register. Nothing was written, and the driver is uninitialised: call EnsureInitialized() , which writes every register again with the outputs before the directions. Now and then: check the expander's supply (decoupling, a load that pulls it down when outputs switch, the ramp in section 8.3), then the bus. After every output change: the outputs draw more current than the supply gives; check the total current limits ( Hardware ). An output does not change ¶ A call returned WriteMismatch : the chip acknowledged the write but did not keep it. Retry (after ToggleOutputs() , with WriteOutputs(GetConfig().output_high_mask) ); if it keeps happening, check the pull-ups, the bus length and noise near the lines, and compare ReadOutputLatch() with GetConfig().output_high_mask . The pin is still an input: SetDirection(mask, Direction::Output) . The port is open-drain (PCAL9555A, SetOutputMode() ): a "high" output floats and needs an external pull-up. A call returned Bus : the write may or may not have arrived. GetConfig() shows the riskier value (a pin that may be an output counts as one, outputs at the written level); the next call reads the register first, and ReadOutputLatch() / ReadInputMask() show what the chip holds. The chip lost power since the start: it is back at its power-up state, every pin an input. CheckForReset() returns DeviceReset ; EnsureInitialized() then writes the driver's copy again. An input reads the wrong level ¶ Polarity inversion is on for the pin ( GetConfig().polarity_invert_mask ). On a PCAL9555A the input is latched ( input_latch_mask ): the read shows the level that raised the interrupt, and the next read shows the pin. A floating input: on the PCAL9555A check pull_enable_mask and pull_up_mask . INT stays low or never falls ¶ Symptom Likely cause Fix Never falls on a PCAL9555A Every pin is masked at power-up SetInterruptEnabled(mask, true) GetLatchedInterrupts() is empty though INT fell The input port was read with ReadRegister() , which clears the status without latching it Use ReadInputs() or ReadPin() , which latch the status first while an input is unmasked Stays low The input port of the pin that raised it was not read ReadInputs() (reads both ports); ReadPin() releases only its own port Falls when a pin becomes an input The data sheet's false interrupt: the pin level differs from the input register Read the inputs once after changing directions Never falls on either part No pull-up on INT, or the pin is an output INT is open-drain; only inputs raise it Bench checks ¶ Hardware-dependent behaviour is not verified on hardware yet. With a PCAL9555A (or PCA9555) at 0x20 on an MCU port, run the ESP32 example or your own code: EnsureInitialized() returns Ok ; a logic analyser shows a read of 0x00 (and of 0x4F for a PCAL9555A), the register writes and their read-backs, each pair in one transfer. An LED on P0_0 follows ToggleOutputs(PinMask(0)) . ReadPin(8) follows a button on P1_0; INT falls on a press and rises after ReadInputs() . A PCA9555 driven with Variant::Pcal9555a fails with Bus (or DeviceIdMismatch ) and the analyser shows no write: this checks the data sheets' silence about unimplemented command bytes. With the address pins at another level, EnsureInitialized() with the default address returns Bus , or NoDevice with a port that has GetLastFailure() (the host example port does; the ESP32 one cannot). GetLatchedInterrupts() keeps a pin after ReadInputs() has released INT, until ClearLatchedInterrupts() . Power-on reset: configure P0_0 as an open-drain output driven low into a load (an LED to VDD through a resistor), then pull the expander's VDD below the power-on reset voltage for longer than the section 8.3 minimum while the MCU keeps running. ReadInputMask() reads 0xFFFF; CheckForReset() returns DeviceReset , and SetDirection(PinMask(8), Direction::Output) returns DeviceReset with the analyser showing one read and no write, and the LED stays off. EnsureInitialized() brings P0_0 back low and open-drain. This checks that a real dip reloads table 4 as the model does.

docs.text: An Agile I/O field of Config differs from its power-up value while variant is Pca9555 . Set variant = Variant::Pcal9555a if a PCAL9555A is fitted, or leave the field at its default.
docs.title: EnsureInitialized returns Unsupported

docs.text: The address is outside 0x20 to 0x27 (an 8-bit address such as 0x40 is the 7-bit 0x20 shifted), or a Config field holds a value that is not an enumerator. Nothing was sent.
docs.title: EnsureInitialized returns InvalidArgument

docs.text: The driver found a register back at its power-up value while its copy says otherwise: the expander went through a power-on reset (a supply dip below the power-on reset voltage, section 6.4), or the chip dropped a write to that register. Nothing was written, and the driver is uninitialised: call EnsureInitialized() , which writes every register again with the outputs before the directions. Now and then: check the expander's supply (decoupling, a load that pulls it down when outputs switch, the ramp in section 8.3), then the bus. After every output change: the outputs draw more current than the supply gives; check the total current limits ( Hardware ).
docs.title: A call returns DeviceReset

docs.text: A call returned WriteMismatch : the chip acknowledged the write but did not keep it. Retry (after ToggleOutputs() , with WriteOutputs(GetConfig().output_high_mask) ); if it keeps happening, check the pull-ups, the bus length and noise near the lines, and compare ReadOutputLatch() with GetConfig().output_high_mask . The pin is still an input: SetDirection(mask, Direction::Output) . The port is open-drain (PCAL9555A, SetOutputMode() ): a "high" output floats and needs an external pull-up. A call returned Bus : the write may or may not have arrived. GetConfig() shows the riskier value (a pin that may be an output counts as one, outputs at the written level); the next call reads the register first, and ReadOutputLatch() / ReadInputMask() show what the chip holds. The chip lost power since the start: it is back at its power-up state, every pin an input. CheckForReset() returns DeviceReset ; EnsureInitialized() then writes the driver's copy again.
docs.title: An output does not change

docs.text: Polarity inversion is on for the pin ( GetConfig().polarity_invert_mask ). On a PCAL9555A the input is latched ( input_latch_mask ): the read shows the level that raised the interrupt, and the next read shows the pin. A floating input: on the PCAL9555A check pull_enable_mask and pull_up_mask .
docs.title: An input reads the wrong level

docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Fix Never falls on a PCAL9555A Every pin is masked at power-up SetInterruptEnabled(mask, true) GetLatchedInterrupts() is empty though INT fell The input port was read with ReadRegister() , which clears the status without latching it Use ReadInputs() or ReadPin() , which latch the status first while an input is unmasked Stays low The input port of the pin that raised it was not read ReadInputs() (reads both ports); ReadPin() releases only its own port Falls when a pin becomes an input The data sheet's false interrupt: the pin level differs from the input register Read the inputs once after changing directions Never falls on either part No pull-up on INT, or the pin is an output INT is open-drain; only inputs raise it
docs.title: INT stays low or never falls

docs.text: Hardware-dependent behaviour is not verified on hardware yet. With a PCAL9555A (or PCA9555) at 0x20 on an MCU port, run the ESP32 example or your own code: EnsureInitialized() returns Ok ; a logic analyser shows a read of 0x00 (and of 0x4F for a PCAL9555A), the register writes and their read-backs, each pair in one transfer. An LED on P0_0 follows ToggleOutputs(PinMask(0)) . ReadPin(8) follows a button on P1_0; INT falls on a press and rises after ReadInputs() . A PCA9555 driven with Variant::Pcal9555a fails with Bus (or DeviceIdMismatch ) and the analyser shows no write: this checks the data sheets' silence about unimplemented command bytes. With the address pins at another level, EnsureInitialized() with the default address returns Bus , or NoDevice with a port that has GetLastFailure() (the host example port does; the ESP32 one cannot). GetLatchedInterrupts() keeps a pin after ReadInputs() has released INT, until ClearLatchedInterrupts() . Power-on reset: configure P0_0 as an open-drain output driven low into a load (an LED to VDD through a resistor), then pull the expander's VDD below the power-on reset voltage for longer than the section 8.3 minimum while the MCU keeps running. ReadInputMask() reads 0xFFFF; CheckForReset() returns DeviceReset , and SetDirection(PinMask(8), Direction::Output) returns DeviceReset with the analyser showing one read and no write, and the LED stays off. EnsureInitialized() brings P0_0 back low and open-drain. This checks that a real dip reloads table 4 as the model does.
